subject: Financial Literacy
title: Priya's Shopping Puzzle
hook: Should you buy everything you want, or only what you need? Priya finds out!

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: a thoughtful student learning to spend wisely

characters.name: Mom
characters.role: Priya's mother who teaches smart spending

slides.title: Priya's Shopping Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Priya learns the difference between what she needs and what she just wants.

image.alt: Priya's Shopping Puzzle — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: The Festival Fair
slides.storyContext: During the local Diwali fair, Priya's mom gives her ₹500. Priya's eyes grow wide—there are so many stalls! Toys, clothes, jewelry, sweets, games, books! Her friend Dev is already running toward the toy stall. But Priya's mom says, 'Wait. Before you spend, let's think about what you NEED versus what you WANT.' Priya is confused: doesn't she need everything that looks fun?

image.alt: The Festival Fair — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: What Are Needs?
slides.storyContext: Mom sits with Priya and explains: 'Needs are things your body and life require to be healthy and safe.'

points.text: Food (rice, bread, vegetables, milk) to stay strong.
Clothes to cover your body and stay warm.
A home to sleep and be safe.
School books and pencils to learn.
Medicine when you're sick.

example.problem: Priya needs new school shoes (hers are worn out). This costs ₹400. Is this a need or a want?
example.solution: A NEED—school shoes protect her feet and are required for school.

slides.inSimpleWords: Needs are things you must have to be healthy, safe, and to do your work or go to school.

image.alt: What Are Needs? — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: What Are Wants?
slides.storyContext: Priya points at a beautiful toy robot on a stall. Mom says, 'That's a WANT. Wants are things you desire but don't truly need.'

points.text: Toys and games you enjoy but don't use every day.
Extra clothes because they look nice (beyond what you wear).
Sweets and snacks (beyond basic food for health).
Movies, fun outings, video games.
Jewelry, fancy items, new gadgets.

example.problem: Priya sees a ₹250 toy robot. She already has toys at home. Is this a need or a want?
example.solution: A WANT—it's nice to have but she doesn't need it to be healthy or safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wants are things that make you happy or entertained but you can live without them.

image.alt: What Are Wants? — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Needs Come First—Smart Spending Rule #1
slides.storyContext: Mom hands Priya a simple rule: 'Every rupee you have should go to needs FIRST. Only spend on wants with leftover money.' Priya nods—this makes sense!

points.text: Priority 1: Buy what you need for health, safety, and learning.
Priority 2: If money is left after needs, then buy a want (if you really want it).
Priority 3: Save any money that's left (for later surprises or emergencies).

example.problem: Priya has ₹500. She needs new shoes (₹400) and school books (₹50). That's ₹450. She wants a toy (₹150). What should she do?
example.solution: First buy needs: ₹400 + ₹50 = ₹450. Left: ₹50. The toy costs ₹150, so she CAN'T afford the want. Better to save the ₹50 or buy a smaller want.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always buy what you need first, then if there's money left, you can spend on wants.

image.alt: Needs Come First—Smart Spending Rule #1 — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: The Trap of Too Many Wants
slides.storyContext: Priya watches Dev at the fair. He buys a toy (₹120), then a game (₹180), then snacks (₹100). He spent ₹400 on things he wanted! By the end, he's out of money and can't buy the winter jacket he actually needs. Mom says gently, 'That's the trap of wants—they add up fast and eat your money.'

points.text: Wants are unlimited—there's always something new and shiny to buy.
If you spend on every want, you'll run out of money for real needs.
Smart spenders pick ONE want they love, not ten small wants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wants are tempting and endless—if you buy many small wants, you'll waste money and not have enough for needs.

image.alt: The Trap of Too Many Wants — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Smart Spending at the Fair
slides.storyContext: Priya decides to be smart. She checks her list: 'I need school shoes (₹400) and new socks (₹50). That's ₹450. I have ₹500 left: ₹50. I could save it, or buy ONE small want like a book (₹40).'

points.text: Make a list of needs BEFORE you go shopping.
Buy needs first—don't get distracted by bright, shiny things.
From leftover money, pick ONE want you really love (not many small wants).
Save the rest for later or emergencies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Make a list, buy needs first, pick one small want if there's money left, and save the rest.

image.alt: Smart Spending at the Fair — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Priya's Smart Shopping (Full Example)
slides.storyContext: Priya goes to the fair with ₹500. She needs: new shoes (₹400), socks (₹50), and wants to buy a book (₹40). How much money does she save?

example.solution: ₹10 saved for later.

image.alt: Priya's Smart Shopping (Full Example) — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Your Turn: Smart Shopping
slides.storyContext: You have ₹300. You need a new school bag (₹200). You want a pencil box (₹50) and a notebook (₹30). Do you have enough? How much is left after buying needs AND one want? Can you buy everything?

example.problem: Needs: ₹200 (bag). Wants: ₹50 (pencil box) + ₹30 (notebook) = ₹80. Total: ₹200 + ₹80 = ₹280. You have ₹300. Left: ?
example.solution: Yes, you can afford everything! Leftover: ₹300 − ₹280 = ₹20.

image.alt: Your Turn: Smart Shopping — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Priya bought her needs, one small want, and saved money. She felt wise and happy!

points.text: Needs are food, clothes, shelter, school, and medicine—things you must have.
Wants are toys, games, snacks, and fun things you enjoy but can live without.
Smart rule: Buy needs FIRST, then one want if money is left, then SAVE.
Don't fall into the trap of many small wants—they add up and waste money.

slides.inSimpleWords: Be smart about money: needs first, one favorite want second, and save the rest.

image.alt: What We Learned — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

subject: English
title: Papa's Spectacles
hook: When Papa's glasses go missing, the whole family searches—and learns that caring for things (and people) matters.

characters.name: Papa
characters.role: A kind father who needs his spectacles to read and work

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: A curious, caring daughter who helps find Papa's spectacles

characters.name: Amma
characters.role: Mother who keeps the household running smoothly

slides.title: Papa's Spectacles
slides.storyContext: A story about a family's search and what we learn when something important goes missing.
slides.inSimpleWords: This story teaches us about caring for the things we use every day and helping our family.

image.alt: Papa's Spectacles — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: The Morning Chaos
slides.storyContext: One morning in their Delhi home, Papa wakes up and cannot find his spectacles. They were on his bedside table last night, but now they have disappeared. Meera hears Papa calling for help and rushes to his room. Amma starts checking the bathroom counter.
slides.inSimpleWords: Papa's glasses are missing! The whole family begins to search everywhere in the house.

image.alt: The Morning Chaos — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: Why Papa Needs His Spectacles

points.label: Papa's job
points.text: Papa is an accountant who works with numbers and papers. He needs his spectacles to see the small figures clearly and avoid making mistakes at work.

points.label: Daily reading
points.text: Every evening, Papa reads the newspaper to know what is happening in the world. Without spectacles, the letters are blurry.

points.label: Helping with studies
points.text: Papa checks Meera's homework by reading her answers carefully. Good spectacles mean he can help her better.

example.problem: Why is it dangerous for Papa to work without his spectacles?
example.solution: Because if he cannot see the numbers clearly, he might write down wrong figures in the company accounts. This could cause big problems for the business and cost money.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spectacles help Papa see clearly, so he can do his job well and help his family.

image.alt: Why Papa Needs His Spectacles — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: Meera's Search Begins

points.label: Checking the bedroom
points.text: Meera looks on the bedside table, under the pillow, and under the bed. She even checks inside Papa's slippers.

points.label: Kitchen and dining table
points.text: Sometimes Papa takes off his spectacles while eating. Meera asks Amma if she has seen them near the dining table or kitchen counter.

points.label: The TV chair
points.text: In the evening, Papa sits in his favorite chair to watch the news. Meera checks behind the cushions and under the armrest.

example.problem: Meera looks in five places but does not find the spectacles. What should she do next?
example.solution: She should make a list of all the places Papa visited yesterday and check each one carefully. She could also ask Papa to remember the last time he remember seeing them clearly.

slides.inSimpleWords: When looking for lost things, think about where we last used them and check those places first.

image.alt: Meera's Search Begins — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: Checking the Medicine Shelf
slides.storyContext: Meera remembers that Papa had a bad headache yesterday evening. He went to the medicine cabinet to get medicine. Maybe he took off his spectacles while he was feeling unwell. Meera climbs on a chair and looks carefully at the shelf where the medicine bottles sit. Behind a bottle of cough syrup, she spots something shiny—gold-rimmed frames!
slides.inSimpleWords: Solving problems often means remembering and thinking like the person who lost the thing.

example.problem: How did Meera use her memory to solve the problem?
example.solution: She remembered that Papa was sick and went to get medicine. She thought: 'Where would someone go if they had a headache?' Then she looked at that place and found the spectacles there.

slides.title: A Close Call
slides.storyContext: Meera is about to celebrate when she realizes the spectacles are still behind the cough syrup bottle. If Amma had knocked the bottle over while cleaning, the spectacles might have fallen and broken. Meera carefully removes them, holding them gently as if they were made of glass—which they are. She wipes them with her dupatta, being very gentle.
slides.inSimpleWords: Finding something is not the end—you must handle it carefully so it does not break.

slides.title: A Lesson in Caring for Things

points.label: Every object has a place
points.text: Papa's spectacles should always go back to the same spot—his bedside table. This way, no one forgets where to find them.

points.label: Things break when we are careless
points.text: Spectacles have glass lenses that can crack or break. If they are left lying around, children might step on them or they might fall.

points.label: Expensive things need respect
points.text: Good spectacles cost a lot of money. Papa had to save up to buy them. When we care for our belongings, we show respect for the money and effort it took to get them.

example.problem: Meera often leaves her school pencils scattered on the table. Why is this careless?
example.solution: Because pencils can break, get lost, or mix with other things. If Meera keeps them in her pencil box in the same place always, she will never lose them and they will last longer.

slides.inSimpleWords: Taking care of our things means keeping them safe in the same place every time.

image.alt: A Lesson in Caring for Things — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: Amma's Organization Tips
slides.storyContext: Amma decides to teach Meera her own organizing methods. 'I label every container and drawer,' she says. 'When I was young, my mother did not teach me this, and I lost so many things. Now I pass this wisdom to you.' Meera watches as Amma labels five different spots in the house for five categories of items.
slides.inSimpleWords: Parents pass down their hard-learned lessons to help their children avoid the same mistakes.

slides.title: The Discovery

points.label: An unexpected place
points.text: Finally, Meera finds the spectacles! They are on the shelf in the living room, next to the medicine cabinet. Papa must have taken them off when he had a headache yesterday.

points.label: The lens is foggy
points.text: When Meera picks them up, she notices the lenses are dusty. This must have happened when Papa set them down quickly while feeling sick.

points.label: Relief and joy
points.text: Papa is so happy! He cleans the lenses gently with a soft cloth and puts them on. Everything is clear again, and he thanks Meera for her patience and careful searching.

example.problem: Why were the spectacles dusty and not on their usual shelf?
example.solution: Because Papa was not feeling well and put them down in a hurry on the medicine shelf, forgetting to move them back to their proper place.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes we forget to put things back where they belong, and that is how we lose them.

image.alt: The Discovery — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: How to Clean Spectacles Properly
slides.storyContext: Papa shows Meera how to clean his spectacles correctly. 'Never rub them dry on your shirt,' he says. 'First, rinse them with lukewarm water. Then use a soft cloth to dry them. Always be gentle because the lenses are delicate.' Meera learns that caring for things means not just finding them, but also maintaining them.
slides.inSimpleWords: The way we care for things can keep them working well for many years.

example.problem: Why should you never rub spectacles dry on your clothes?
example.solution: Because cloth can have tiny dust particles that can scratch the lenses. Rinsing with water first removes dust, and a special soft cloth protects the lenses.

slides.title: Steps to Protect Fragile Items
slides.storyContext: Papa teaches Meera a system for protecting delicate things like spectacles.

points.label: Use a case or box
points.text: Spectacles should always be kept in a case, not left on open tables where they can be knocked over.

points.label: Keep them away from heat and moisture
points.text: Leaving spectacles in the sun, near a hot stove, or in a humid bathroom can damage the lenses and frames.

points.label: Handle with clean hands
points.text: Dirty hands can transfer oil and dust to the lenses, making it harder to see clearly.

slides.inSimpleWords: Caring for spectacles means protecting them from heat, moisture, dust, and rough handling.

slides.title: Caring for Others Shows Love

points.label: Meera helps without complaining
points.text: Meera could have been upset about searching everywhere, but instead she spent her time helping Papa. This shows she loves him and cares about his well-being.

points.label: Amma's support
points.text: Even though Amma is busy with her morning chores, she stops to help search. When we help our family, we show that we care.

points.label: Papa's gratitude
points.text: Papa thanks Meera and gives her a hug. He says that having a caring family is more valuable than any pair of spectacles.

example.problem: What did Meera learn about her family by searching for Papa's spectacles?
example.solution: She learned that her family cares about each other and will stop whatever they are doing to help when someone needs them. She also learned that showing love means taking action to solve problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: Helping someone we love, even when it takes time, shows how much we care about them.

image.alt: Caring for Others Shows Love — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: The New System
slides.storyContext: After the spectacles are found, the family decides to create a system to never lose important things again. Papa puts a small basket on his bedside table labeled 'Before Sleep.' Meera creates a poster for her room: 'One Place, Every Time.' Even Amma joins in, creating labels for where keys, purses, and other important items should always go. Soon, the whole house is organized.
slides.inSimpleWords: Creating systems prevents problems before they happen.

example.problem: What would you put in a 'One Place, Every Time' system in your home?
example.solution: House keys should hang on a hook by the door. Schoolbag should rest in the corner of the bedroom. Shoes should sit in the shoe rack. When everything has a home, nobody loses anything important.

slides.title: A Worked Example: Lost and Found
slides.storyContext: Let us solve this problem like Meera did. Yesterday, Meera's school notebook went missing. It has her homework in it.

example.problem: Meera's notebook is missing. She checked her school bag, her desk, and her shelf, but it is not there. Where should she look next? How can she remember where she might have left it?
example.solution: Step 1: Think about where she used the notebook last. She used it during her study time in the evening, then she did her homework. Step 2: Ask herself: Did she carry it to any other room? Did she leave it on the dining table? Did someone borrow it? Step 3: Check the places where she spent time that day—her bedroom, the living room, Amma's kitchen, even near the TV. Step 4: Ask her family members if they saw it. This is how Meera found her notebook under the sofa cushion, where it had fallen while she was studying.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find something lost, remember where you used it last and check places where you spent time.

image.alt: A Worked Example: Lost and Found — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: Different Types of Things Need Different Care

points.label: Fragile things (spectacles, phones)
points.text: These have delicate parts. They need soft cases, gentle handling, and should never be left in hot places or wet places.

points.label: Valuable things (jewelry, watches)
points.text: These should be kept in a safe place, locked if needed, and only taken out when needed.

points.label: Daily-use things (schoolbag, shoes, lunch box)
points.text: These need a fixed spot near the door or in your room, so you never forget them when you leave home.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different types of objects need different types of care based on what they are and how often we use them.

slides.title: The Morning Papa Forgot Twice
slides.storyContext: A week after finding his spectacles, Papa leaves them on the newspaper while he reads the morning news. Amma almost vacuums them up! Meera laughs and gently rescues them. 'Papa,' she says, 'even you need to practice putting things in their place!' Papa smiles, humbled by the lesson.
slides.inSimpleWords: Even after learning a lesson, it takes practice to build new habits.

slides.title: Papa Shares His Wisdom
slides.storyContext: Over dinner, Papa tells Meera and Amma: 'When I was a boy, my father lost his watch. He was so upset. He taught me then that losing important things teaches us to be more careful. But more importantly, it teaches us that objects are just objects. People matter most. You both were willing to spend your morning helping me find my spectacles. That is what made me truly happy.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Losing things teaches us that relationships and family are more precious than any object.

slides.title: Real Situation: The Lost Phone
slides.storyContext: Meera's friend Priya loses her mother's mobile phone. She remembers the lesson from Papa's spectacles and thinks carefully.

example.problem: Priya's mother's phone went missing. She last used it in the living room three hours ago. Where should Priya look?
example.solution: First: What did Mother do after using the phone? She might have moved to the kitchen, the bedroom, or the bathroom. Second: In the kitchen, Priya checks the counter near the cooking area. Third: In the bedroom, she checks the bed and the charging table. She finds it on the bed, where her mother set it down to rest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Using a logical system like Meera's helps you find lost things quickly.

slides.title: Your Turn: Think and Solve
slides.storyContext: Now it is your turn. Imagine this: Your father's watch has gone missing at home. He wears it every day to work. Think about what you would do and why it is important to find it. Write two sentences about where you would search and what this teaches you about caring for others.

example.problem: Where would you look for a missing watch, and what does searching for it teach you about being a caring family member?
example.solution: I would check places where Papa takes off his watch: near the bathroom sink (where he washes his hands), his bedside table, his office desk at home, and the dining table. I would also ask Amma and others if they saw it. Searching teaches me that caring for someone means being patient and thoughtful, and that helping find important things is a way of showing love and respect. It also teaches me the importance of always keeping things in their proper place so we don't lose them.

slides.inSimpleWords: Being a caring family member means helping find lost things and remembering to keep important items safe.

image.alt: Your Turn: Think and Solve — Papa's Spectacles

slides.title: Create Your Own 'One Place' System
slides.storyContext: Think about your home and the things your family uses every day. What gets lost most often? Is it keys, schoolbags, glasses, or something else? Design a simple system to make sure these things never get lost.

example.problem: How would you design a system for your home that makes sure nothing important ever goes missing?
example.solution: First, list five things that often go missing at home. Second, pick a specific spot for each thing near where it is used most—keys by the door, schoolbag in the bedroom corner, glasses on the bedside table. Third, label each spot or make a poster. Fourth, test the system for one week and see if it works. If something still gets lost, move that item's spot and try again.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can help your family by creating a system that keeps important things safe and organized.

slides.title: The Lesson Spreads
slides.storyContext: Meera tells her best friend Priya about finding Papa's spectacles and the new organization system at home. Priya's mother had just lost her reading glasses yesterday! Priya suggests to her mother the same method: check all the places where she usually takes them off. Her mother finds them on the kitchen shelf next to the recipe book. Soon, three more families in the neighborhood adopt the system. What started as Meera's problem has become a lesson for the whole community.
slides.inSimpleWords: Good solutions spread when we share them with others and help our community learn.

slides.title: The True Value of Responsibility
slides.storyContext: As Meera watches her family members carefully put their important items in their designated places each evening, she understands something deep.

points.label: Responsibility means caring ahead of time
points.text: It is not just about finding lost things. It is about creating habits so things do not get lost in the first place.

points.label: Small actions prevent big problems
points.text: Taking five seconds to put spectacles in the right place saves hours of searching later.

points.label: Teaching others is part of responsibility
points.text: When Meera tells Priya about the system, she helps Priya's family avoid the same stress Papa experienced.

slides.inSimpleWords: True responsibility is about taking care of things every day, not just fixing problems after they happen.

slides.title: Test Your Responsibility
slides.storyContext: Think of one precious item in your home that gets lost often. What would be your plan to never lose it again?

example.problem: My schoolbag often goes missing. How can I fix this?
example.solution: Pick one specific spot: the corner of my bedroom. Every single day after school, I put it there. On weekends, it stays there too. After two weeks, this becomes a habit, and I never lose my bag again.

slides.inSimpleWords: Building a habit requires picking ONE place and using it every single time.

slides.title: One Year Later
slides.storyContext: A year has passed. Papa still uses the same spectacle case on his bedside table. The 'One Place, Every Time' poster hangs on Meera's bedroom wall. Amma smiles every time she sees Meera carefully putting her schoolbag in its corner. The family has never lost anything important again. And whenever a neighbor mentions losing something, they know exactly where to go for advice: to the family who learned the hard way.
slides.inSimpleWords: Building good habits today saves stress and solves problems before they happen tomorrow.

slides.title: Why Habits Work Better Than Rules

points.label: Habits are automatic
points.text: When you brush your teeth before bed every night, you do not have to think about it—your body just does it. Good habits work the same way.

points.label: Rules need thinking
points.text: A rule says 'Put your spectacles away.' But you have to remember it every time. A habit is when you do it without thinking.

points.label: 21 days makes a habit
points.text: Scientists say that repeating an action for 21 days turns it into a habit. After that, it feels natural.

slides.inSimpleWords: Habits are more powerful than rules because they work automatically without thinking.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.label: Important objects need care
points.text: Things like spectacles and watches help us do our work and live our daily lives. We must keep them safe.

points.label: A place for everything
points.text: If we always put things back in the same spot, we will never lose them. This is the first rule of caring for belongings.

points.label: Family helps each other
points.text: When someone needs help finding something important, the whole family works together. This shows love and unity.

points.label: Patience and care matter
points.text: Taking time to search carefully, asking questions, and thinking logically helps us solve problems. This is how Meera found Papa's spectacles.

points.label: Caring is an action
points.text: Showing care is not just saying nice words. It is about doing things that help the people we love, even when it takes effort.

points.label: Systems prevent problems
points.text: Creating routines and organizing our spaces helps prevent many problems before they even happen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Papa's Spectacles teaches us that caring for things and caring for our family go together. When we keep important things safe and help each other, we make our home a happy and organized place.

image.alt: What We Learned — Papa's Spectacles

subject: English
title: Gone with the Scooter
hook: A boy's brand-new scooter goes missing, teaching him about friendship, greed, and taking things that don't belong to you.

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: boy who receives a new scooter and learns a hard lesson

characters.name: Amar
characters.role: poor boy from the neighborhood who admires the scooter

characters.name: Mr. Sharma
characters.role: the shopkeeper who knows what happened

slides.title: Gone with the Scooter
slides.storyContext: A story about why taking what is not yours is wrong, even if you really want it.

image.alt: Gone with the Scooter — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: Vikram's Special Gift
slides.storyContext: It is Vikram's birthday. His parents give him a bright red Bajaj scooter with chrome handles. Vikram is so happy he rides it around the neighbourhood all day. But he leaves it outside the market when he stops to buy ice cream.
slides.inSimpleWords: Vikram gets a wonderful new scooter but forgets to lock it properly.

image.alt: Vikram's Special Gift — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: Property: What Is Yours and What Isn't

points.label: Your property
points.text: Something is yours if your parents bought it for you, or you earned money to buy it yourself.

points.label: Someone else's property
points.text: If someone else owns it, you do not have the right to use it without asking—even if you want it badly.

points.label: Taking without asking is stealing
points.text: Even if you think you will return it, taking something without permission is a crime.

slides.inSimpleWords: What belongs to someone else is not yours to take, no matter how much you want it.

image.alt: Property: What Is Yours and What Isn't — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: Amar's Hard Life
slides.storyContext: Amar lives two streets away. His father left the family when Amar was small. His mother works at the market selling vegetables, but the money is never enough. Amar's school uniform has patches. His schoolbag was his older cousin's, secondhand. Every morning, he walks two kilometers to school in the hot sun. He has never asked for anything, knowing his mother cannot afford it.
slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes children understand their family's struggles and try not to add to their burden.

example.problem: Why does Amar not tell his mother he wants a scooter?
example.solution: Because he knows his mother works very hard just to buy food and pay rent. Asking for expensive things would only make her sad and worried.

slides.title: Amar's Wish
slides.storyContext: Amar is Vikram's classmate. He lives in a small house near the railway line. His family is poor. He walks to school every day. When he sees Vikram's red scooter, his eyes light up. That night, Amar dreams of riding it fast through the streets.

points.label: Wanting something is natural
points.text: It is okay to wish for things. Many children want a scooter, bicycle, or mobile phone.

points.label: But wishing does not give you the right
points.text: Just because you want something does not mean you can take it from someone else.

points.label: Envy can lead to bad choices
points.text: If you let your wish grow into envy (wanting what others have), you might do something you regret.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wishing for something is okay, but letting that wish turn into greed can push you to steal.

image.alt: Amar's Wish — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: The Night of Temptation
slides.storyContext: For two weeks, Amar watches Vikram ride the scooter every afternoon. Vikram never offers to let Amar try it. One night, Amar cannot sleep. The image of the red scooter keeps playing in his mind. He thinks: 'Just one ride. Just one night. I will bring it back before anyone knows.' He knows it is wrong, but his heart is burning with longing. At midnight, he creeps out of his house.
slides.inSimpleWords: Strong desires can push us to make choices we know are wrong.

slides.title: When Desire Becomes Temptation
slides.storyContext: Amar stands outside Vikram's house, looking at the scooter parked in the yard. His hands are shaking.

points.label: Temptation is a feeling
points.text: Temptation is when we really want something and feel like taking it, even though we know it is wrong.

points.label: Our conscience warns us
points.text: Inside, a small voice tells us: 'This is stealing. Do not do it.' But if we ignore that voice long enough, it gets quieter.

points.label: One moment of weakness changes everything
points.text: Amar's decision to steal in the next few seconds will change his entire life—his reputation, his family, his future.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you feel tempted to do something wrong, listen to your conscience—that quiet voice telling you right from wrong.

slides.title: The Scooter Goes Missing
slides.storyContext: When Vikram goes to fetch his scooter the next morning, it is gone. The lock has been cut. Vikram runs home crying. His mother calls the police. The police ask questions. Vikram feels terrible—his beautiful gift has vanished. Days pass. Vikram walks to school sadly, watching everyone else ride scooters and bicycles.

points.label: The real damage of theft
points.text: It is not just about the scooter. Vikram loses trust in his neighbourhood. He feels unsafe. His family worries.

points.label: Pain spreads wider
points.text: The thief harms not just one person, but everyone around them—parents, police, neighbours, and community.

points.label: Loss of innocence
points.text: Vikram learns that people he knows might not be trustworthy. This saddens him and makes him less open and friendly.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you steal, you hurt not just the owner, but everyone who cares about them.

image.alt: The Scooter Goes Missing — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: The Many Types of Stealing

points.label: Shoplifting
points.text: Taking items from a store without paying is the most common type of theft children commit.

points.label: Taking from a friend
points.text: Taking money, toys, or belongings from friends is theft, even if you plan to return it.

points.label: Taking from home
points.text: Taking money from a parent's purse or a sibling's savings is also stealing, and it breaks family trust.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stealing comes in many forms, but all types are wrong and carry consequences.

slides.title: Amar Rides at Midnight
slides.storyContext: Amar rides the scooter through empty streets in the middle of the night. For the first time, he feels the wind on his face, feels the speed, feels alive and free. He rides for two hours, up to the big bridge on the highway, through the quiet market, past the sleeping shops. Every moment is precious. But each moment is also stolen. Each moment weighs heavy on his heart.
slides.inSimpleWords: Even the happiness from a stolen thing carries the burden of guilt.

slides.title: Amar's Secret Burden
slides.storyContext: It was Amar who took the scooter. He rode it in the middle of the night, faster than he had ever gone. For two days, he felt happy. But then guilt started to eat at him. He could not sleep. Every time he saw Vikram's sad face at school, he felt worse. His mother noticed he was not eating. 'Beta, what is wrong?' she asked. Amar could not tell her.

points.label: Guilt is a heavy burden
points.text: A stolen thing brings no real joy. The guilt of stealing ruins your peace and health.

points.label: Lying makes it worse
points.text: Amar has to lie to his mother, lie at school, lie to everyone. Each lie adds weight to his guilt.

points.label: Insomnia and fear
points.text: Amar cannot sleep because he is afraid the police will come. He cannot enjoy the scooter because every ride feels like a crime.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stealing something does not make you happy because guilt eats away at your happiness from inside.

image.alt: Amar's Secret Burden — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: The Weight Gets Heavier
slides.storyContext: Three days pass. Amar hides the scooter in a locked room behind his house. He tells his mother he is not feeling well and stays home from school. He does not even want to ride the scooter anymore. All he can think about is Vikram's tears and the police walking through the neighborhood asking questions.
slides.inSimpleWords: The longer you hide a wrong action, the heavier the weight of guilt becomes.

slides.title: The Discovery
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma, the shopkeeper, sees Amar riding the scooter early one morning. He knows Amar's family and knows he could never afford such a scooter. He calls the police. Amar is caught. The scooter is returned to Vikram. But now Amar is in trouble—his parents are ashamed, the school has been told, and Vikram does not trust him anymore.

points.label: Consequences are real
points.text: Amar faces punishment, shame, and the loss of his reputation in school.

points.label: The friendship is broken
points.text: Even after the scooter is returned, Vikram and Amar can no longer be friends. The trust is gone.

points.label: The cost far exceeds the want
points.text: Amar risked his future, his family's respect, and his friendship for a few days of riding a scooter.

points.label: His mother's pain
points.text: Amar's mother cried when she heard what her son did. She works so hard to teach him right from wrong, and now the whole neighborhood judges him as a thief.

slides.inSimpleWords: Getting caught does not just mean losing the object—it means losing your reputation and relationships.

image.alt: The Discovery — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: Understanding the Root: Why Do Children Steal?
slides.storyContext: Amar did not steal because he was a bad person. He stole because he felt left out. He saw other children with bicycles and scooters, and he felt ashamed of walking. He wanted to belong. He wanted just one day of feeling like he was as good as the richer children.

example.problem: A child steals a toy from a richer friend's house. Is the child bad, or are there deeper reasons?
example.solution: Usually, there are deeper reasons: feeling poor, feeling left out, wanting to fit in. But this does not excuse the theft. The answer is to talk to parents and teachers about these feelings, not to steal. Schools can also help by making sure all children feel included and valued.

slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding WHY a child steals helps us teach them a better way to handle feeling poor or left out.

image.alt: Understanding the Root: Why Do Children Steal? — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: The Difference Between Borrowing and Stealing

points.label: Borrowing is asking first
points.text: When you borrow, you ask the owner's permission. You say when you will return it. The owner knows and agrees.

points.label: Stealing is taking without permission
points.text: When you steal, you take something without asking. The owner does not know. You plan to keep it or plan to return it in secret.

points.label: Even intending to return is stealing
points.text: Amar planned to return the scooter the same night. But that does not make it borrowing. It is still stealing because he did not ask.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stealing and borrowing seem similar, but they are completely different. Borrowing is honest; stealing is a crime.

slides.title: Amar Meets the Police
slides.storyContext: The police officer sits down with Amar in a small room at the police station. 'Amar,' the officer says gently, 'stealing is a serious crime. When you turn eighteen, this will become part of your record. It will affect which schools accept you, which jobs hire you, your entire future.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Theft has consequences that can follow you for years, affecting your opportunities and your life.

slides.title: Vikram's Lesson in Kindness
slides.storyContext: A month after the scooter is returned, Vikram's mother suggests he think about why Amar stole. 'He did not steal because he was evil,' she says. 'He stole because he felt poor and left out.' Vikram realizes that showing kindness to children from poorer families costs him nothing but means everything to them.
slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding why someone did something wrong helps us respond with wisdom instead of anger.

slides.title: Your Challenge
slides.storyContext: You see your best friend has brought an expensive gaming device to school. You have been wanting one for months, but your parents say they cannot afford it right now. The device is left on the desk while your friend is in the toilet. You could take it, hide it, and say it was stolen. What should you do?

example.problem: You want something your friend has. You have a chance to take it without getting caught. What is your choice?
example.solution: You should NOT take it. Instead, talk to your friend: 'I wish I had one too. Can you teach me how to play on yours sometimes?' Or tell your parents: 'I really want this. Can we save up?' Both choices are honest and keep your friendship alive.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wanting something is okay. Stealing it is not. Ask, wait, or talk about your wish instead.

image.alt: Your Challenge — Gone with the Scooter

slides.title: Amar's Mother Teaches a Lesson
slides.storyContext: After Amar is caught, his mother sits with him and says: 'Beta, you brought shame to our family. But you are still my son, and I will help you learn from this. However, I will not forgive you easily. You must work to rebuild trust.' Amar spends the next three months doing extra chores without pocket money, showing his remorse.
slides.inSimpleWords: Parents who truly love their children will punish them to teach them right from wrong.

slides.title: What Would You Do? The Second Chance
slides.storyContext: Imagine Amar had gone to Vikram BEFORE taking the scooter. He could have said: 'Your scooter is so cool. I wish my family could afford one. Could I please ride it just once, with your permission?' What would happen then?

example.problem: What do you think Vikram would have done if Amar had asked politely instead of stealing?
example.solution: Many children who are asked politely will share. Vikram might have said yes, or he might have said no. But if he said yes, Amar would ride without guilt and without fear. If he said no, Amar's heart would be sad, but his reputation would be clean, and his family would be proud. Some things worth having are worth waiting for or worth earning.

slides.inSimpleWords: Asking politely, even when you expect a no, is always better than stealing and living in fear.

slides.title: Amar's Punishment and Reflection
slides.storyContext: The police do not charge Amar because of his age and because this was his first crime. But the school suspends him for a week. His mother makes him apologize to Vikram's parents. Most importantly, Amar learns a harsh lesson: one moment of greed cost him his friend, his reputation, his mother's trust, and his peace of mind. He will carry this shame for a long time.
slides.inSimpleWords: The consequences of stealing are much more painful than any happiness the stolen thing could bring.

slides.title: Better Ways to Get What You Want
slides.storyContext: Instead of stealing, there are honest ways to get the things you wish for.

points.label: Ask and explain
points.text: Tell the person why you want to use their thing. Be honest about your feelings. Many people respond to honesty with kindness.

points.label: Save up or work
points.text: If your parents say no, ask if there are chores you can do to earn money. Many children have bought their own bicycles and scooters this way.

points.label: Wait for special occasions
points.text: Birthdays and festivals are times when parents are more likely to buy expensive gifts. Saving these wishes for those times shows patience.

slides.inSimpleWords: Asking, earning, and waiting are hard, but they keep you honest and help you get what you want without guilt.

slides.title: Manage Your Own Wants
slides.storyContext: You want many things, but you cannot have them all. How do you decide which wants are worth working for?

example.problem: I want a gaming device, a bicycle, and new shoes. My parents say I can earn money for one thing. Which should I choose and why?
example.solution: Think about what you NEED first (shoes if yours are broken) versus what you WANT (gaming device). Then think about what you would use most often. The bicycle gets used daily, so it is worth the effort. Finally, ask yourself: 'Will working hard to earn this teach me something good?' The answer for a bicycle is yes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Smart choices come from thinking about needs, frequency of use, and what you will learn.

slides.title: The Neighborhood's New Rule
slides.storyContext: After the incident, Vikram's parents decide to teach their son about sharing and kindness. Once a month, Vikram invites two neighborhood children to ride the scooter for an hour. He realizes that owning a beautiful thing is better when he can see joy on other faces too. Amar is not invited, but he watches from far away and knows the price of his choice.
slides.inSimpleWords: Sharing what you have brings real happiness, while stealing what others have brings only shame.

slides.title: How to Help a Friend Who Steals

points.label: Do not cover for them
points.text: If a friend steals and asks you to lie for them, say no. Real friends tell each other the truth.

points.label: Encourage them to confess
points.text: Tell them: 'This is wrong, but confessing is the right choice. It will be hard, but honesty is the best path.'

points.label: Stay their friend but hold them accountable
points.text: Friendship does not mean accepting bad behavior. It means caring enough to tell them they are wrong.

slides.inSimpleWords: True friendship means being honest with friends about their mistakes, not helping them hide.

slides.title: The Law and Stealing

points.label: Stealing is a crime
points.text: In every country, taking something that does not belong to you without permission is illegal. Police investigate theft.

points.label: Consequences grow with age
points.text: A child who steals might face school punishment. A teenager might face juvenile court. An adult faces jail time.

points.label: A criminal record lasts forever
points.text: Even if you are young, a theft conviction stays on your record, affecting college admission and job opportunities.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stealing is not just wrong—it is against the law, and breaking the law has serious consequences.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Stealing is taking something that belongs to someone else without permission.
Just because you want something does not mean you can take it.
Theft harms not just the owner, but the whole community and the thief's own peace of mind.
Guilt is a heavy burden that no stolen object can make lighter.
The best way to get what you want is to work, save, ask nicely, or talk about your feelings honestly.
Stealing breaks friendships and ruins reputations in ways that cannot be fully repaired.
Some stolen things give temporary happiness, but they take away permanent peace.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stealing always has a high price—higher than the cost of the thing you took.

image.alt: What We Learned — Gone with the Scooter

subject: English
title: The Rainbow
hook: A curious boy asks his grandmother why a rainbow appears after rain, and learns science through storytelling and wonder.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: curious boy who asks questions about nature

characters.name: Nani (Grandmother)
characters.role: wise storyteller who explains nature and science

slides.title: The Rainbow
slides.storyContext: A story about natural phenomena, light, and the wonder of asking questions.

image.alt: The Rainbow — The Rainbow

slides.title: After the Storm
slides.storyContext: It is June, the monsoon season in Mumbai. Rain falls hard for an hour. The streets flow with water. Then, suddenly, the clouds break. Sunlight pours down. Arjun runs to the balcony and gasps. Stretched across the sky from one building to another is a perfect rainbow—red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple bands, so vivid they look like they are painted.
slides.inSimpleWords: After heavy rain, when sun and water meet, nature paints a rainbow in the sky.

image.alt: After the Storm — The Rainbow

slides.title: What Is a Rainbow?

points.label: Not a solid object
points.text: A rainbow is not a bridge or a solid thing. It is light bending through water droplets in the air.

points.label: Light and water work together
points.text: Sunlight enters raindrops, bends inside them, reflects, and bends again as it comes out. This creates the colored bands.

points.label: You can never reach the end
points.text: The rainbow is always the same distance away from you. If you walk toward it, it moves away. If you drive toward it, it is always far.

slides.inSimpleWords: A rainbow is sunlight playing with water droplets in the sky—not a thing you can touch.

image.alt: What Is a Rainbow? — The Rainbow

slides.title: Arjun's First Question
slides.storyContext: Arjun stares at the rainbow with wide eyes. 'Nani!' he calls to his grandmother, who is sitting inside watching the rain from the window. 'Come quick! There is a rainbow! How does it appear? Is it magic? Can I touch it?' Nani smiles and puts on her glasses. She has been waiting for this question her whole life. She knows that every child who asks about the rainbow is beginning to understand nature.
slides.inSimpleWords: Every natural wonder has a scientific explanation waiting to be discovered.

example.problem: Why do you think rainbows only appear after rain?
example.solution: Because rainbows need two things: water droplets in the air (from rain) and sunshine at the right angle. Without rain, there are no droplets. Without sun, there is no light to bend.

slides.title: The Colors and Their Order
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Nani: 'Why are the colors always in the same order? Red is always on top, and purple is always at the bottom.' Nani smiles and says: 'Because light is made of different colors, and each color bends at a slightly different angle. Red bends the least, so it stays on the outer edge. Violet bends the most, so it stays on the inside.'

points.label: ROYGBV (Remember this order)
points.text: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet. This order never changes because it is based on light physics.

points.label: Refraction is the science word
points.text: When light bends as it moves through water, we call it 'refraction.' Different colors bend differently.

slides.inSimpleWords: The colors are always in the same order because each color bends at its own special angle.

image.alt: The Colors and Their Order — The Rainbow

slides.title: The Tiny Water Droplet's Journey
slides.storyContext: Nani tells Arjun a story about a single raindrop. 'Imagine a tiny water droplet falling from the clouds. Sunlight from behind you hits this droplet. The light enters the droplet, bounces inside like a ball in a curved room, and comes out. As it bounces inside, it splits into all its colors. Red comes out at one angle, orange at a slightly different angle, blue at another angle. Millions of droplets do this at once, and together they create the rainbow you see.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A rainbow is millions of water droplets, each one splitting sunlight into its seven colors.

slides.title: How Light Enters and Exits a Droplet
slides.storyContext: Let us trace exactly what happens to one beam of sunlight as it enters a raindrop.

example.problem: Sunlight hits the outside of a raindrop. What happens next?
example.solution: Step 1: The light enters the curved surface of the droplet and bends (refracts). Step 2: The light travels through the clear water inside the droplet. Step 3: When it hits the back of the droplet, it bounces (reflects) like light bouncing off a mirror. Step 4: It travels toward the front again. Step 5: When it exits, it bends again. Each color bends at its own angle, so red exits at one direction, violet at another, creating the rainbow bands.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light enters the droplet, bounces inside, and exits bent at different angles for each color.

slides.title: Why Rainbows Need Both Sun and Rain

points.label: Sunlight must shine while it rains
points.text: The sun must be behind you, and rain must be falling in front of you. This is why rainbows usually appear late afternoon after a monsoon.

points.label: The angle matters
points.text: The sun must be at the right angle (usually less than 42 degrees above the horizon) for a rainbow to appear. At noon, with the sun high, there is no rainbow.

points.label: Three things at once
points.text: Sun, water droplets, and your eye all must line up perfectly. This is rare and beautiful.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rainbows only appear when the sun, rain, and your eyes are in the right place at the same time.

image.alt: Why Rainbows Need Both Sun and Rain — The Rainbow

slides.title: Double Rainbows and Secondary Rainbows
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices that sometimes, outside the main rainbow, there is a fainter, second rainbow. The colors in the second rainbow are in reverse order—violet on the outside, red on the inside. 'Is there a third rainbow, Nani?' Arjun asks. 'There can be,' Nani says, 'but it is so faint that only the clearest skies and perfect angles let us see it. The world is full of secrets if you watch carefully.'

points.label: Secondary rainbows are real
points.text: Light can bounce inside a raindrop twice. Each bounce spreads the light wider and makes it fainter.

points.label: Colors reverse in the secondary rainbow
points.text: This is because the light is reflecting an extra time inside the water droplet.

points.label: Nature has layers
points.text: What looks simple—a rainbow—is actually full of hidden science if you look closely.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes you can see a fainter second rainbow outside the first one, with the colors upside down.

image.alt: Double Rainbows and Secondary Rainbows — The Rainbow

slides.title: Rainbows in Unexpected Places
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Nani walk to the nearby park after the rain stops. Near the fountain, Arjun spots a tiny rainbow in the water spray! He points and laughs. 'Nani, the fountain made a rainbow!' Nani nods. 'Yes, beta. Rainbows are not only in the sky. Wherever light bends through water, you can find them.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rainbows can appear in fountains, waterfalls, and even in spray bottles on sunny days.

slides.title: Angle of Incidence and Refraction

points.label: The sun's angle matters
points.text: The sun must be at an angle of less than 42 degrees above the horizon. If the sun is higher, light rays bounce away from your eye.

points.label: Your position relative to the sun
points.text: You must always have the sun behind you and rain in front of you. This creates the geometry needed for a rainbow.

points.label: Why rainbows are 42 degrees
points.text: Due to the physics of light refraction and reflection inside a water droplet, the rainbow always appears at this specific angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rainbows only appear when the sun is at the correct angle and you are positioned between the sun and the rain.

slides.title: Rainbows Around Us (Not Just in the Sky)
slides.storyContext: Nani takes Arjun to the kitchen. She holds a glass of water up to the sunlight coming through the window. 'Look!' A tiny rainbow appears on the kitchen wall. Arjun laughs. 'It is the same thing!' Yes, he understands now. Wherever light bends through water or glass, rainbows can form.

points.label: Prisms make rainbows
points.text: A prism is any object that can bend light—a glass of water, a crystal, a water droplet. All can make rainbows.

points.label: Waterfalls create rainbows too
points.text: Near waterfalls or fountains on sunny days, you can often see rainbows formed the same way.

points.label: Oil on water makes rainbows
points.text: The rainbow colors on a puddle of spilled petrol are light bending through a thin film—another form of nature's light show.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rainbows form anywhere light bends through water or clear objects—not just in the sky.

image.alt: Rainbows Around Us (Not Just in the Sky) — The Rainbow

slides.title: Arjun's Experiment
slides.storyContext: Arjun becomes so excited about rainbows that he decides to do an experiment. He fills a spray bottle with water and sprays it in the garden on a sunny afternoon. Sure enough, a tiny rainbow appears in the spray. He sprays it from different angles and watches the rainbow move. 'Nani!' he shouts. 'I made a rainbow!' Nani hugs him. 'No, beta. You did not make the rainbow. You created the conditions for it to appear. The sun was always there. The water was always there. You just brought them together.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Science is about understanding how nature works and creating the right conditions to see it.

slides.title: Experiment: Make Your Own Rainbow
slides.storyContext: Now you can try what Arjun did. On a sunny day, find a place outside where the sun is shining from behind you.

example.problem: How can you create a rainbow in your garden using a water spray bottle?
example.solution: Step 1: Stand with the sun behind you. Step 2: Face away from the sun. Step 3: Spray water gently in front of you toward the area where the sun shines through the spray. Step 4: Look for a small rainbow in the mist. Step 5: Adjust the angle and distance until the rainbow is most vivid. You have now made the conditions for a rainbow, and light does the rest!

slides.inSimpleWords: You can make rainbows appear by combining water spray and sunlight at the right angle.

slides.title: Why Scientists Study Rainbows
slides.storyContext: Nani explains: 'Scientists do not study rainbows just because they are beautiful. They study them to understand how light works. Understanding light led to inventions like cameras, microscopes, and telescopes. A rainbow is nature's way of teaching us about light.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Studying natural phenomena like rainbows helps us invent new technologies.

slides.title: A Real Example: The Monsoon Rainbow of Cochin
slides.storyContext: During the Kerala monsoon, after afternoon storms, rainbows often stretch over the backwaters near Cochin. Local fishermen say that if you see two rainbows at once, the day's catch will be good. Whether or not this is true, the beauty of the double rainbow reminds them of nature's power and precision.

example.problem: Why do rainbows appear more often during the monsoon season in India?
example.solution: During monsoon (June to September), heavy rains fall almost daily, and the sun often shines briefly between showers. This creates ideal conditions: sun behind you, rain in front. In winter, the skies are clearer, so rain and sun rarely occur together.

slides.inSimpleWords: Monsoons bring many rainbows because rain and sun take turns throughout the day.

image.alt: A Real Example: The Monsoon Rainbow of Cochin — The Rainbow

slides.title: Why White Light Is Actually Seven Colors

points.label: Light is not really white
points.text: Sunlight is made of seven colors mixed together: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. When all mixed, they look white.

points.label: Different colors have different wavelengths
points.text: Red light has the longest wave, violet has the shortest. This is why they bend at different angles.

points.label: This is why grass looks green
points.text: Grass absorbs all colors of light except green. Green bounces back to our eyes, so we see green.

slides.inSimpleWords: All the colors we see are hidden inside white sunlight, waiting to be revealed by a raindrop.

slides.title: Color Absorption and Reflection
slides.storyContext: Nani explains: 'Look around the garden. The flowers are red. Why? Because the flower petals absorb blue and green light but reflect red light back to our eyes. A book looks blue because it absorbs other colors and reflects blue. Everything you see is light bouncing back at specific wavelengths.'
slides.inSimpleWords: We see colors because objects absorb some light and reflect the rest back to our eyes.

slides.title: Your Challenge: Predict and Observe
slides.storyContext: You are standing in a garden after rain. The sun is shining from behind you, and you see a faint rainbow forming across the garden. How would you explain to a younger child why the rainbow appears at that exact spot and not somewhere else?

example.problem: If you move to a different part of the garden, does the rainbow move with you, or does it stay in the same place?
example.solution: The rainbow always moves with you! The water droplets that make the rainbow are at a fixed angle from the sun and your eye. If you move, that angle changes, and a different set of water droplets creates the rainbow you see. So every observer sees their own unique rainbow.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each person sees their own rainbow. If you walk sideways, your rainbow walks with you.

image.alt: Your Challenge: Predict and Observe — The Rainbow

slides.title: Design Your Own Rainbow Experiment
slides.storyContext: Now it is your turn to create the conditions for a rainbow, like Arjun did. Think about what you need: sunlight, water, and the right angle. How would you create a rainbow using things in your home or garden?

example.problem: What are three ways you could make a rainbow appear using water and sunlight?
example.solution: 1. Spray water from a hose in the garden on a sunny afternoon, standing with the sun behind you. 2. Hold a glass of water up to sunlight through a window and tilt it until a rainbow appears on the wall. 3. Run a tap gently in sunlight and look for tiny rainbows in the water spray. All three work because they create water droplets where sunlight can bend through them.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can create rainbows yourself by bringing together water and sunlight in the right way.

slides.title: When Rainbows Do Not Appear
slides.storyContext: Arjun waits by the window one afternoon hoping to see a rainbow. It rains, and the sun comes out, but no rainbow appears. 'Nani, why is there no rainbow?' he asks. Nani explains: 'The angle is not right. The sun is too high, and the rain is too far away. Sometimes all three things line up perfectly, and sometimes they do not. That is why rainbows are rare treasures.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Not all rain brings rainbows because the conditions have to be exactly right.

slides.title: The Legend and the Science
slides.storyContext: Nani tells Arjun an old story: 'In the old days, people did not know about light and refraction. They made up stories about rainbows. Some said rainbows were bridges to heaven. Some said they were the gods' jewelry. Some said they predicted good harvests or bad times.' Arjun asks: 'Were they wrong, Nani?' Nani smiles. 'No, beta. They were right in their hearts. A rainbow IS a kind of magic—the magic of science, the magic of nature's laws working perfectly. Understanding the science does not take away the wonder. It adds to it.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding how rainbows work makes them even more beautiful, not less.

slides.title: Light Wavelengths and Human Vision
slides.storyContext: Different colors have different wavelengths, and that is why our eyes see them as different colors.

points.label: Red light has the longest wavelength
points.text: Red light waves are about 700 nanometers. They bend the least when passing through water.

points.label: Violet light has the shortest wavelength
points.text: Violet light waves are about 400 nanometers. They bend the most when passing through water.

points.label: Our eyes detect wavelengths as colors
points.text: The cones in our eyes respond to different wavelengths and send signals to the brain, which interprets them as colors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different light colors have different wavelengths, and our eyes translate these differences into the colors we see.

slides.title: Arjun Teaches Others
slides.storyContext: Arjun becomes so fascinated by rainbows that he starts a 'Rainbow Club' at school. He teaches his friends how to make rainbows with spray bottles and explains the science. Some children are amazed by the explanation. Others just love the beauty of the rainbows themselves. Arjun realizes that science and wonder are not opposites—they go together.
slides.inSimpleWords: Sharing what you learn about nature brings joy to others and deepens your own understanding.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Rainbows form when sunlight bends and reflects inside water droplets.
The colors always appear in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
Rainbows need sun, rain, and your eye all in the right place at the same time.
Secondary rainbows are fainter and have colors in reverse order.
Rainbows appear wherever light bends through water—not just in the sky, but in prisms, waterfalls, and puddles too.
White sunlight is actually made of seven colors mixed together.
You can create rainbows yourself if you understand the science behind them.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rainbows are nature's light show, and they teach us that science is hiding in the beauty around us.

image.alt: What We Learned — The Rainbow

slides.title: The Physics of Refraction

points.label: Light travels in straight lines
points.text: In empty space, light always travels in a straight line. But when it enters water, it slows down.

points.label: Slower speed causes bending
points.text: When light hits water and slows down, it bends toward the normal (an imaginary perpendicular line). This is refraction.

points.label: Different wavelengths bend differently
points.text: Because different colors have different wavelengths, they slow down by different amounts, causing them to separate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bends when it enters water, and each color bends at its own angle.

slides.title: Rainbows Across Cultures
slides.storyContext: Nani tells Arjun: 'In old Indian stories, rainbows were called Indra's bow, named after the king of the gods. In Western stories, they were bridges to fairy lands. Different cultures have different names, but everyone sees the same colors in the same order, because light obeys the same laws everywhere.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rainbows are universal—people everywhere see them the same way because light follows the same rules.

slides.title: Observe and Record
slides.storyContext: Keep a rainbow journal. Every time you see a rainbow, write or draw: the time, the weather, where you were, and what you saw. After collecting five rainbows, analyze your data.

example.problem: What patterns do you notice about when and where rainbows appear?
example.solution: You will notice that all your rainbows appeared in the late afternoon (3-5 PM), after rain, with the sun low in the sky behind you. You might notice rainbows near water (river, waterfall, garden spray) more often than in open fields. This is real scientific observation!

slides.inSimpleWords: Observing and recording patterns is how scientists learn from nature.

subject: English
title: What a Tank!
hook: A boy learns about water conservation when an old village water tank teaches him how precious water really is.

characters.name: Rohan
characters.role: city boy visiting his village grandfather

characters.name: Grandfather
characters.role: village elder who teaches water wisdom

characters.name: Riya
characters.role: village girl who knows water scarcity firsthand

slides.title: What a Tank!
slides.storyContext: A story about water, waste, and why we must respect this precious resource.

image.alt: What a Tank! — What a Tank!

slides.title: Rohan Discovers the Old Tank
slides.storyContext: Rohan comes to his grandfather's village for the summer. In Mumbai, water flows from the tap whenever he turns the handle. In the village, he finds an ancient concrete tank in the courtyard—cracked, half-full of murky water, covered with moss and algae. 'Grandfather, why is this disgusting thing here? Can't you install a modern water filter, like in the city?' His grandfather smiles sadly. 'Beta, this tank is the heart of our village. Without it, we have no water at all.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rohan arrives from the city where water seems endless, but in the village, water is saved drop by drop.

image.alt: Rohan Discovers the Old Tank — What a Tank!

slides.title: Water from the Tap at Home
slides.storyContext: Rohan thinks back to his life in Mumbai. Every morning, he showers with hot water from a tap. He brushes his teeth with running water. His mother uses taps for cooking, cleaning, washing clothes. At his apartment, there is a large water tank on the terrace, but it is refilled automatically by a truck every week. If it runs empty, they simply call the water company. Water is not precious in Mumbai—it is abundant, taken for granted, almost free.

slides.title: Why Villages Need Water Tanks

points.label: No piped water in most villages
points.text: Villages rely on wells, tanks, and seasonal rainfall. They cannot call the water department if water runs out.

points.label: Tanks store water for dry months
points.text: During May and June before the monsoon, wells dry up. The tank must hold enough water for the whole community to survive.

points.label: Sharing one source
points.text: A village tank serves hundreds of people—for drinking, cooking, bathing, and watering livestock. Everyone depends on it.

slides.inSimpleWords: In villages, water tanks are not a luxury—they are the difference between having water and suffering thirst.

image.alt: Why Villages Need Water Tanks — What a Tank!

slides.title: The Math of Scarcity
slides.storyContext: Grandfather shows Rohan a simple calculation. 'In the city, you use 100 litres of water per day—baths, flushing toilets, washing clothes, drinking. Here, we have 2,000 litres in the tank. That must serve 50 people for the whole month. So each person gets... how much per day?' Rohan counts: 2,000 ÷ 50 ÷ 30 = about 1.3 litres per person per day. He is shocked. 'But I use that much just for one bath!' His grandfather nods.

points.label: Urban water per person: ~100 litres/day
points.text: In cities, we often use 80-150 litres per person daily, much of it wasted.

points.label: Rural water per person: 10-20 litres/day
points.text: In water-scarce villages, people use only what they absolutely need: drinking, cooking, basic washing.

points.label: The gap is a privilege problem
points.text: The difference is not just geography—it is wealth, infrastructure, and access to power to pump water.

slides.inSimpleWords: City people use 5 to 10 times more water per day than villagers, often without realizing it.

image.alt: The Math of Scarcity — What a Tank!

slides.title: Early Morning at the Well
slides.storyContext: Rohan wakes at 4 a.m. to the sound of women's voices outside. He peers from the window and sees Riya and her mother, along with dozens of village women, walking toward the well in the darkness with empty buckets and pots. 'Come,' his grandfather says, 'let us see what Riya's morning is like.' They walk to the well. It is already crowded. The water level is low—barely knee-deep. Women are filling buckets one by one, rationing how much each family gets. Riya carries two 20-litre pots on her head, one in each hand. Rohan tries to lift one—it is impossibly heavy. Riya laughs: 'I do this every morning before school. By the time I reach school, I am tired.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Getting water in a village is hard work, not the simple turn of a tap.

example.problem: How much physical work is it to fetch water for a family of five in a village?
example.solution: Each person needs about 20 litres per day (drinking, cooking, basic washing). A family of five needs 100 litres. Carrying 20-litre pots on your head multiple times daily is equivalent to exercising for an hour. Children (especially girls) miss school or arrive tired. This is unpaid household labour.

slides.title: What Happens When the Tank Empties
slides.storyContext: Riya, a girl from the village who is Rohan's age, invites him to walk to the well with her before dawn. 'We must go early,' she says, 'before the sun heats the ground and the water is already warm. And before other families get there.' They arrive at 5 a.m. Already, 20 women and girls are waiting, buckets in hand. Water is low. Each person gets only three buckets for the whole day. Riya fills hers quickly, balancing one on her head while carrying the others. Rohan is amazed. His mother uses three buckets just for one load of laundry.

points.label: Rationing becomes a daily routine
points.text: When water is scarce, it must be shared fairly. Families gather in order. It becomes a community ritual.

points.label: Women and girls pay the highest price
points.text: Fetching water is traditionally women's work. Girls miss school because they must spend hours carrying water.

points.label: Limited water changes everything
points.text: Cooking, bathing, washing clothes, and sanitation all compete for the same scarce litres.

slides.inSimpleWords: When a tank runs dry, a whole village suffers. Women especially carry the burden.

image.alt: What Happens When the Tank Empties — What a Tank!

slides.title: The Dry Summer
slides.storyContext: May arrives, and the heat is unbearable. The tank is now only 20 percent full. Grandfather sits with Rohan and explains: 'Three years ago, we had a drought. The monsoon failed. No rain for eight months. Our tank dried completely. People had to walk 3 kilometres to a neighbouring village to fetch water. Some families left to find work in the city. Riya's youngest brother got dysentery from drinking contaminated well water. We almost lost him.' Rohan realizes the tank is not just about convenience—it is about life and death.

slides.title: Riya's Brother and Disease
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks about Riya's brother now. Grandfather explains: 'He recovered, but the village learned a harsh lesson. When the main tank is empty, people dig small wells or drink from ponds. That water is not clean. Bacteria from animals and sewage get in. Children get sick with dysentery, cholera, typhoid. In a city, we have water treatment and sewers. Here, everything is connected—dirty water spreads disease fast.' Rohan sees Riya's brother playing outside, healthy now, and feels grateful.

slides.title: Clean Water vs. Contaminated Water

points.label: Clean water = safe to drink and cook with
points.text: Free from bacteria, viruses, and chemicals that cause disease.

points.label: Contaminated water = can kill or seriously sicken
points.text: Just one bacterium can multiply into millions and cause dysentery, typhoid, or cholera.

points.label: Tanks prevent contamination
points.text: A covered, sealed tank protects water from animal waste and pollution. An open well or pond is a disease risk.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dirty water spreads disease. Clean water saves lives. This is why tanks are life-or-death infrastructure.

slides.title: The Monsoon Gift
slides.storyContext: June arrives. The monsoon rains begin. Rohan watches as rain pours into the tank. After weeks of scarcity, the tank is almost full again. But Grandfather warns: 'These rains must last us through May next year. If the monsoon is weak this year, we will suffer next summer.' He shows Rohan how water leaks from a small crack in the tank. 'Every drop lost here is a drop we do not have in June. So we must fix this.'

points.label: Monsoon is seasonal
points.text: Most Indian rain falls in 3-4 months (June-September). The water collected must last 8-9 dry months.

points.label: Leaks are serious
points.text: A small leak that seems harmless wastes thousands of litres over months, making the difference between survival and thirst.

points.label: Planning for drought
points.text: Villagers must think years ahead. A weak monsoon today means hardship tomorrow.

slides.inSimpleWords: Monsoon rain is seasonal. It must be saved carefully to last through the dry months.

image.alt: The Monsoon Gift — What a Tank!

slides.title: Tank Maintenance Day
slides.storyContext: Grandfather takes Rohan to help clean the tank. Young men from the village are scrubbing the concrete bottom, removing algae and debris. 'The tank must be clean,' Grandfather explains, 'or the water becomes diseased. Every monsoon, we clean it. Every year, we patch cracks. Every five years, we rebuild parts of it. This tank was built in 1960. We have maintained it for over 60 years. Our children and their children will maintain it.' Rohan sees the work that goes into something invisible—maintenance is a skill, a sacrifice, and a gift to the future.

slides.title: The Algebra of Tank Maintenance
slides.storyContext: Grandfather asks Rohan to solve a problem: 'This tank holds 2,000 litres and serves 50 people. If we lose 10 litres to leaks per day, how many litres do we lose in 30 days? How many people does that water feed?' Rohan calculates: 10 × 30 = 300 litres lost per month. 300 ÷ 20 (per person per day) ÷ 30 days = 0.5 person's water supply. So the leak starves one family every two months. 'You see,' Grandfather says, 'fixing a small leak is as important as building a new well.'

example.problem: A tank with 2,000 litres serving 50 people has a leak of 10 litres per day. How many people lose water in six months due to the leak?
example.solution: 10 L/day × 180 days = 1,800 litres lost in six months. 1,800 L ÷ 20 L per person = 90 person-days of water lost, or about 3 people's supply for a month. A small leak starves families. Fix it immediately.

slides.title: Water Wisdom: How to Waste Less
slides.storyContext: Grandfather teaches Rohan the village ways: take quick showers (one bucket of water), not long showers; fetch water at dawn to avoid walking in the heat; reuse water from washing clothes to water plants; keep a large pot to catch water while waiting for hot water. Every drop has a purpose. When Rohan returns to Mumbai, he tries to apply these lessons at home—shorter showers, fixing leaky taps, using a bucket instead of running water. His mother notices and asks what changed. 'Grandfather taught me that water is not free. Someone has to work hard for it. And there may not be enough forever.'

points.label: One-bucket bathing
points.text: Fill a bucket of water and use it to wash, instead of standing under a running tap. This reduces water use from 40 litres to 5 litres per bath.

points.label: Rainwater harvesting
points.text: Collect monsoon water in tanks to store for dry months. Every house can do this.

points.label: Fix leaks immediately
points.text: A dripping tap wastes up to 1,000 litres per month. Fix it and you save water like digging a new well.

slides.inSimpleWords: Small changes—shorter baths, fixing leaks, catching rainwater—save enough water to fill many tanks.

image.alt: Water Wisdom: How to Waste Less — What a Tank!

slides.title: The School's New Tank
slides.storyContext: Riya tells Rohan that the school recently built a rainwater harvesting tank. Water collected from the school roof during monsoon fills a tank that can supply drinking water for the whole school year. This means students no longer have to walk 2 kilometres to fetch water during exams and summer study sessions. The headmaster says the tank will also be used to teach children about water conservation. 'This one tank,' the headmaster says, 'changes everything—girls stay in school, we have water for sanitation, and children understand water is precious.'

slides.title: Girls' Education and Water Access
slides.storyContext: Riya confesses to Rohan: 'I missed school 20 days last year because I had to fetch water. My marks dropped. I almost failed mathematics. The school officials said I was lazy.' Now with the school's new tank, she drinks at school and does not have to wake at 4 a.m. to fetch water before sunrise. 'This one tank means I can study more, sleep more, be healthier, and stay in school. My parents hope I can now score better and maybe go to college. Water is not just a commodity—it is the key to my future.'

slides.title: Calculate Your Own Water Use
slides.storyContext: Rohan tries to calculate his own water use in Mumbai. One bath with a running shower: 40 litres. Flushing the toilet: 5 litres per flush, 10 flushes per day = 50 litres. Washing hands and brushing teeth: 10 litres. Doing laundry: 100 litres. Drinking and cooking: 5 litres. Total: about 205 litres per day, just for Rohan alone.
