Amir sees vertical bars for each fruit. Bananas have the tallest bar (19), so they sold best. Oranges have the shortest bar (8). 'So bananas are our winner!' exclaims Neha.

points.label: Bar Graph
points.text: Uses vertical (or horizontal) bars to compare quantities

points.label: Axis Labels
points.text: X-axis (horizontal) shows categories (mangoes, bananas, etc.), Y-axis (vertical) shows the count

points.label: Bar Height/Length
points.text: Represents the value for each category; taller/longer bar = larger quantity

points.label: Reading Bars
points.text: Look at where the top of each bar aligns with the scale on the Y-axis

example.problem: A bar graph shows fruit sales: Mangoes bar reaches 13, Bananas bar reaches 19, Oranges bar reaches 8, Apples bar reaches 25. Which fruit was the most sold? Which was the least sold?
example.solution: Most sold: Apples (25). Least sold: Oranges (8).

slides.inSimpleWords: A bar graph uses tall or short bars to compare numbers. Taller bar = bigger number.

slides.title: Amir Draws His First Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Amir takes grid paper and carefully draws two lines—one across (X-axis) and one up (Y-axis). Along the bottom, he writes: Mangoes, Bananas, Oranges, Apples. Up the side: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Now for each fruit, he colors squares from the bottom up to match the count. Neha cheers, 'It's perfect!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Drawing a bar graph: Start with two perpendicular lines. Label them, then fill squares up to each value.

slides.title: Creating Your Own Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Amir decides to make his own bar graph on grid paper. He writes the fruit names along the bottom (X-axis) and numbers (0–30) along the side (Y-axis). For each fruit, he colors in squares from the bottom up to the number sold. Neha checks his work: 'Perfect! Now anyone can see that bananas and apples are our bestsellers.'

points.label: Step 1: Draw Axes
points.text: Draw a horizontal line (X-axis) and vertical line (Y-axis)

points.label: Step 2: Label Axes
points.text: X-axis gets categories (fruit names); Y-axis gets numbers (count scale)

points.label: Step 3: Draw Bars
points.text: For each category, draw a bar reaching up to the correct number

points.label: Step 4: Color/Shade
points.text: Fill or color the bars so they stand out; add a title

example.problem: You have data: Apples 12, Bananas 18, Grapes 10, Oranges 15. Create a bar graph with X-axis labeled with fruit names and Y-axis numbered 0–20.
example.solution: Draw four bars: Apples bar to 12, Bananas bar to 18, Grapes bar to 10, Oranges bar to 15. Ensure each bar's top aligns with its number on the Y-axis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Making a bar graph: draw two lines (axes), label them, then draw bars for each category up to its number.

slides.title: Comparing Two Weeks
slides.storyContext: After two weeks of tracking, Amir makes two bar graphs side by side. 'Look! Week 1 shows more oranges than Week 2. But Week 2 has more apples!' Neha calculates: 'Week 1 total: 13+19+8+25 = 65 fruits. Week 2 total: 15+22+6+28 = 71 fruits. Week 2 was bigger!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Bar graphs help us see patterns over time and understand when things change.

slides.title: Comparing and Interpreting Graphs
slides.storyContext: Amir's father looks at the bar graph and says, 'So we sold 25 apples and 19 bananas, but only 8 oranges. That means people prefer apples and bananas. Maybe I should buy more apple trees!' Neha adds, 'And we know exactly how much more: 25 − 8 = 17 more apples than oranges.'

points.label: Comparison
points.text: Bar graphs let us compare quantities at a glance (which is biggest, smallest, equal)

points.label: Finding Differences
points.text: Subtract one value from another (e.g., 25 − 8 = 17 more apples than oranges)

points.label: Finding Totals
points.text: Add all bars together to find total sales (e.g., 13 + 19 + 8 + 25 = 65 total fruits)

points.label: Making Decisions
points.text: Data guides real-world choices (stock more of bestsellers, less of slow items)

example.problem: Bar graph shows: Monday 12 customers, Tuesday 18 customers, Wednesday 10 customers, Thursday 15 customers. How many more customers came on Tuesday than Wednesday? What was the total for the week so far?
example.solution: Tuesday − Wednesday = 18 − 10 = 8 more customers on Tuesday. Total = 12 + 18 + 10 + 15 = 55 customers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs help us compare and make real decisions. We can see which is biggest, find differences, and add totals.

slides.title: Pictograph vs. Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Mr. Verma teaches Amir and Neha: 'Pictographs are fun and easy to draw quickly. Bar graphs are exact and easier to compare heights. Use pictographs for quick stories. Use bar graphs for precise data.' Amir nods, 'So a pictograph is like a story, a bar graph is like math!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Both pictographs and bar graphs show data, but each is best for different purposes.

slides.title: Choosing the Right Graph
slides.storyContext: Neha has data from a school survey: 'Which subject do you like best?' Results: Math 28, English 22, Science 35, History 15. Should she make a pictograph or bar graph? Mr. Verma says, 'Bar graph is better—the numbers are large and precise.'

example.problem: You have these survey results: Chocolate 40, Vanilla 25, Strawberry 20, Mango 35. Would you make a pictograph or bar graph? Why? Create the bar graph with the numbers.
example.solution: Bar graph is better (numbers are all over 20). Draw Y-axis 0–45, X-axis with flavors, and bars: Chocolate 40, Vanilla 25, Strawberry 20, Mango 35.

slides.inSimpleWords: When numbers are large or exact, use a bar graph. When telling a simple story, pictographs work well.

slides.title: A Week of Market Data: The Full Story
slides.storyContext: Amir and Neha collect data for an entire week and present it to Mr. Verma. They create both a pictograph and a bar graph. Mr. Verma studies them carefully and says, 'Excellent work! Now I see the real story of my market. Let's use this to plan next month.'

example.problem: Weekly fruit sales: Mon (M=5, B=7, O=3, A=8), Tue (M=6, B=9, O=4, A=10), Wed (M=4, B=5, O=2, A=6), Thu (M=7, B=10, O=5, A=12), Fri (M=8, B=12, O=6, A=14). Create a pictograph using symbols where 1 symbol = 2 fruits. Also, calculate total apples sold for the week.
example.solution: Monday total: 5+7+3+8 = 23 fruits. Tuesday total: 6+9+4+10 = 29 fruits. Wednesday total: 4+5+2+6 = 17 fruits. Thursday total: 7+10+5+12 = 34 fruits. Friday total: 8+12+6+14 = 40 fruits. Total apples for week: 8+10+6+12+14 = 50 apples. Pictograph: Each day gets symbols for each fruit type, with each symbol representing 2 fruits.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real data from a week tells a big story. Both pictographs and bar graphs help us see patterns and trends.

image.alt: A Week of Market Data: The Full Story — Data Through Pictures

slides.title: Mystery: Which Fruit Wins?
slides.storyContext: Neha challenges Amir: 'I've made a bar graph of sales for the last 10 days, but I mixed up the labels! Bananas, Oranges, Apples, and Mangoes are jumbled. The bar heights are 10, 18, 12, and 25. Can you figure out which fruit is which based on what we know sells best?'

example.problem: Four bars show: 10, 18, 12, and 25. Based on the previous week's data (Apples were highest, Oranges were lowest), assign fruit names to each bar.
example.solution: Most likely: Apples = 25 (highest), Bananas = 18, Mangoes = 12, Oranges = 10 (lowest). This matches the pattern from last week where apples were popular and oranges sold the least.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes we need to use patterns and logic to read graphs, not just the numbers.

slides.title: Create Your Own Pictograph
slides.storyContext: Now Amir and Neha want to make a pictograph for the next week's data. The numbers are: Mangoes 20, Bananas 15, Oranges 10, Apples 25. They must decide: what should each picture symbol mean?

example.problem: Design a pictograph for: Mangoes 20, Bananas 15, Oranges 10, Apples 25. Choose a symbol value (1 picture = ?, 1 picture = 5?, etc.) and decide how many pictures to draw for each fruit.
example.solution: If 1 picture = 5 fruits: Mangoes 4 pictures, Bananas 3 pictures, Oranges 2 pictures, Apples 5 pictures. If 1 picture = 10 fruits: Mangoes 2 pictures, Bananas 1.5 pictures, Oranges 1 picture, Apples 2.5 pictures.

slides.inSimpleWords: When making a pictograph, pick a symbol value that gives you 2-5 pictures per row (not too many, not too few).

slides.title: Data Prediction Game
slides.storyContext: Amir looks at three weeks of data. Week 1: Apples 15. Week 2: Apples 20. Week 3: Apples 25. Neha predicts: 'Week 4 will be 30!' Is she right? What pattern do we see?

example.problem: See the pattern: Week 1 = 10 items, Week 2 = 15 items, Week 3 = 20 items, Week 4 = ?. What's the pattern, and what will Week 4 be?
example.solution: The pattern is +5 each week. Week 4 = 20 + 5 = 25 items.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look for patterns in data over time. If numbers grow by the same amount each time, you can predict the next one.

slides.title: A Real-World Use
slides.storyContext: Amir's father decides to use their graphs to stock the shop. 'Based on your data, I'm ordering more apples, fewer oranges, and medium bananas and mangoes. Your graphs just saved me money and helped my customers!' Amir feels proud that data made a real difference.
slides.inSimpleWords: Data graphs aren't just exercises—they help real businesses and people make smart decisions.

slides.title: The Market Data Story
slides.storyContext: At the end of the week, Amir's father thanks both children. 'You've taught me to see my business through data. I now know exactly which fruits to stock and which to reduce. That's the power of data!' Neha smiles: 'And it all started with simple pictures and bars.'

points.label: Tally Marks
points.text: Help us count data quickly using groups of 5

points.label: Pictographs
points.text: Use pictures and symbols to show data; each picture has a fixed value

points.label: Bar Graphs
points.text: Use vertical or horizontal bars to compare quantities

points.label: Interpreting Data
points.text: We can compare (bigger, smaller), find differences, and make real decisions based on graphs

points.label: Data in Real Life
points.text: Markets, schools, hospitals use graphs to make smart choices

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs turn numbers into pictures. Pictures make it easy to understand data and make good decisions.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Explore Their School
hook: Two friends discover how a school brings everyone together to learn and grow.

slides.title: Our School - A Happy Place
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya walk into their school on the first day of the term.

slides.title: Welcome to School!
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya feel a mix of excitement and nervousness. Mr. Sharma greets them at the gate with a warm smile. 'Come, let me show you around,' he says. 'Our school is like a big family where everyone learns, plays, and grows together.'

slides.title: What is a School?
slides.storyContext: As they walk through the hallways, Mr. Sharma explains: 'A school is a place where students come to learn new things.'

points.text: A school is a building where children gather to study and learn.
Teachers guide students in understanding subjects like Mathematics, Science, and English.
Schools have classrooms, libraries, playgrounds, and other facilities.

slides.inSimpleWords: A school is a special place where we learn important things and make friends.

slides.title: A Tour of Wonderful Places
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma walks Ravi and Priya through the school. 'Every corner is important,' he says. 'The classroom is where we learn. The playground is where we grow strong. The library is where we discover worlds in books. The office is where the principal guides us all.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A school has many special areas, and each one helps us learn and grow in different ways.

slides.title: Different Roles in School
slides.storyContext: Priya asks, 'Who are all these people here?' Mr. Sharma points around: 'Everyone has an important job.'

points.label: Teachers
points.text: Help students learn subjects and solve problems.

points.label: Principal
points.text: Leads the school and makes sure everything runs smoothly.

points.label: Librarian
points.text: Takes care of books and helps students find information.

points.label: Helpers/Support Staff
points.text: Keep the school clean and safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every person in school—teachers, principal, helpers—works together to make it a good place for learning.

slides.title: Meet the Principal
slides.storyContext: They visit the principal's office. The principal is kind and listens carefully. 'I make sure every student is happy, safe, and learning well,' she says. 'If you ever have a problem or need help, my door is always open.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The principal is the leader of the school and cares about every student's wellbeing.

slides.title: A Teacher's Day
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows his classroom. 'I wake up early, plan lessons, prepare materials, then teach you math, science, and more. After school, I mark your work and prepare for tomorrow. It takes dedication!'

example.problem: If Mr. Sharma teaches for 5 hours at school and spends 2 hours preparing at home every day, how many hours per day does he spend on teaching and preparation?
example.solution: 5 + 2 = 7 hours per day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Teachers work hard both in class and outside to help us learn well.

slides.title: School Rules and Routines
slides.storyContext: As the bell rings at 9 a.m., Ravi notices everyone moves to their classrooms. 'We follow routines,' Mr. Sharma says, 'so learning happens smoothly for everyone.'

points.text: School starts and ends at set times.
We follow rules: listening in class, raising hands to speak, being on time.
There are times for lessons, breaks, lunch, and play.
Rules keep everyone safe and happy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Schools have rules and a daily schedule so everyone knows what to do and when.

slides.title: Why Rules Matter
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks, 'Why do we need all these rules?' Mr. Sharma explains: 'Rules keep us safe, help us respect each other, and make sure everyone can learn. If we all raised our voices at once, no one could hear. If we didn't line up, people would push. Rules are like invisible helpers.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rules aren't meant to stop fun—they're meant to keep everyone safe and happy.

slides.title: A Perfect School Day Schedule
slides.storyContext: Priya looks at the daily timetable: 8:45 Arrival, 9:00 Assembly, 10:00 Class 1, 11:00 Break, 11:15 Class 2, 12:15 Lunch, 1:00 Class 3, 2:00 Sports, 3:00 Class 4, 3:30 Dismissal.

example.problem: If Class 1 is from 10:00 to 11:00, and there's a 15-minute break, when does Class 2 end if it's also 1 hour long?
example.solution: Class 2 starts at 11:15 and lasts 1 hour, so it ends at 12:15.

slides.inSimpleWords: A school day has a careful schedule so each activity gets the right amount of time.

slides.title: Learning Subjects and Skills
slides.storyContext: Priya peeks into a classroom where students are solving math problems. 'What subjects do we study?' she asks. Mr. Sharma smiles: 'Many important ones!'

points.label: Mathematics
points.text: Numbers, shapes, and problem-solving.

points.label: Science
points.text: Understanding animals, plants, weather, and how things work.

points.label: English/Languages
points.text: Reading, writing, and speaking clearly.

points.label: Social Studies
points.text: Learning about people, places, history, and geography.

slides.inSimpleWords: In school, we study many subjects to learn about the world and become smart and curious.

slides.title: Math Class Adventure
slides.storyContext: Ravi loves math. Today, the class is learning about fractions by cutting pizzas! 'One slice is 1/4 of a pizza,' Mr. Sharma explains. 'Four slices make one whole. Math is everywhere—in food, sports, money, and building!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Math isn't just numbers on paper—it's in real life, helping us understand and solve problems.

slides.title: The School Playground
slides.storyContext: At noon, Ravi and Priya run to the playground. Children play cricket, badminton, and games. 'This is where we grow stronger,' Ravi says happily.

points.text: Playgrounds have space for games and sports.
Playing makes our bodies strong and healthy.
Games teach teamwork, fairness, and following rules.
Play time is just as important as study time.

slides.inSimpleWords: A school playground is where we play games, exercise, and have fun while becoming healthier.

slides.title: Teamwork on the Field
slides.storyContext: During cricket, Ravi's team wins because they communicate and support each other. 'Sports teach more than just winning,' Mr. Sharma says. 'They teach you to listen, work together, respect opponents, and get up when you fall.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Sports and games teach us life lessons beyond just fun and exercise.

slides.title: Sports Numbers
slides.storyContext: The school volleyball tournament: Boys' team scored 25 points, Girls' team scored 23 points. In cricket, Ravi's team scored 45 runs, and the other team scored 38 runs.

example.problem: How many more points did the boys' volleyball team score than the girls' team? How many more runs did Ravi's cricket team score?
example.solution: Volleyball: 25 − 23 = 2 points more for boys. Cricket: 45 − 38 = 7 more runs for Ravi's team.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even sports involve counting, comparing scores, and understanding numbers.

slides.title: Library - The House of Books
slides.storyContext: Next, they visit the library. Rows of colorful books line the shelves. The librarian shows them how to borrow books. 'Here, you can find stories, knowledge, and adventure,' she says.

points.text: A library has many books on different topics.
We can borrow books to read at home and return them later.
Libraries help us learn beyond textbooks.
Quiet and peaceful reading space is important in a library.

slides.inSimpleWords: A library is like a treasure chest of books that help us explore new ideas and stories.

slides.title: The Magic of Reading
slides.storyContext: Priya finds a book about space. 'Wow, astronauts travel to the moon!' She reads for an hour, completely lost in the story. The librarian smiles: 'That's the magic of books—they take us anywhere, anytime.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Books open doors to worlds we've never imagined and teach us things beyond our experience.

slides.title: Special Activities and Clubs
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows them a notice board. 'We have art club, science club, sports, music, and drama. Every student can join activities they love and discover new talents!'

points.text: Art club develops creativity and expression.
Science club explores experiments and discoveries.
Music and drama clubs build confidence.
Clubs let students explore interests beyond regular subjects.

slides.inSimpleWords: Schools offer clubs and activities so every student can find something they love and grow in new ways.

slides.title: Priya Joins Drama Club
slides.storyContext: Priya is nervous but joins the drama club. In her first play, she acts as a village girl selling flowers. When the audience claps, she feels proud and confident. 'I didn't know I could do this!' she tells Mr. Sharma.
slides.inSimpleWords: Trying new activities at school helps us discover talents and become more confident.

slides.title: A Day in School
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma gives them a schedule: '8:45 a.m.—arrive at school. 9:00 a.m.—morning assembly and flag hoisting. 10:00 a.m.—English class. 11:00 a.m.—break (15 min). 11:15 a.m.—Math class. 12:15 p.m.—Science. 1:15 p.m.—lunch. 2:00 p.m.—sports. 3:00 p.m.—art and crafts. 3:30 p.m.—assembly and dismissal.'

example.problem: If Ravi's English class starts at 9:00 a.m. and lasts 1 hour, what time does it end?
example.solution: 9:00 a.m. + 1 hour = 10:00 a.m. English class ends at 10:00 a.m.

slides.title: Your School Challenge
slides.storyContext: Now it's time for Ravi and Priya to think: 'How can we be good students and make our school happier?'

example.problem: Write three ways you can help make your school a happy place.
example.solution: 1. Listen to teachers and follow rules. 2. Be kind to friends and help others. 3. Keep the school clean and take care of books and materials.

slides.title: Design a Perfect Timetable
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya are asked to design a timetable for their school day. They must include math, English, science, lunch, break, sports, and art—and fit it all into 6 hours!

example.problem: Create a school day timetable from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. (6 hours total) that includes: Math (1 hour), English (1 hour), Science (1 hour), Lunch (30 min), Break (15 min), Sports (45 min), and Art (30 min). How much time is left over?
example.solution: Total needed: 1+1+1+0.5+0.25+0.75+0.5 = 5.5 hours. 6 − 5.5 = 0.5 hours (30 minutes) left for morning assembly or additional activity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Planning a schedule requires thinking about how much time each activity needs.

slides.title: School Survey: What Do Students Think?
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya decide to survey their classmates: 'What's your favorite subject?' They collect data: Math 12, English 8, Science 18, Art 7. Create a bar graph!

example.problem: Survey results: Math 12, English 8, Science 18, Art 7. Draw a bar graph and find: Which subject was most popular? How many more students preferred Science over English?
example.solution: Bar graph shows Science has the tallest bar. Science − English = 18 − 8 = 10 more students preferred Science.

slides.inSimpleWords: We can use graphs to understand what other students think and prefer.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they leave school that day, Ravi and Priya feel excited about coming back tomorrow.

points.text: A school is a place for learning, playing, and growing.
Teachers, principal, helpers, and librarians all help run the school.
School has rules, routines, and subjects we study.
Playgrounds and libraries are important parts of a school.
Every student can help make the school happy and safe.
Clubs and activities help us discover new talents and interests.
School is our learning home where friends and teachers help us grow.

slides.inSimpleWords: School is our learning home where friends and teachers help us grow into thoughtful, smart people.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Discover India
hook: Two friends explore India's diverse cultures, languages, festivals, and people across many states.

slides.title: Our Vibrant Country
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit their grandmother's house and ask her stories about India.

slides.title: The Land of Diversity
slides.storyContext: Grandma spreads a big map of India on the floor. 'Look, this is our country,' she says. 'From north to south, east to west, we have so many different people, languages, foods, and festivals. That's what makes India special—unity in diversity.'

slides.title: India - Our Country
slides.storyContext: Priya traces the outline: 'How big is India?' Grandma smiles: 'India is a large country in South Asia with 28 states and 8 union territories.'

points.text: India is the world's largest democracy.
Its capital city is New Delhi.
India is surrounded by oceans: the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, and Indian Ocean.
The Himalayan Mountains are in the north.

slides.inSimpleWords: India is a big, beautiful country where many different people, religions, and languages live together in peace.

slides.title: A Journey from Mountains to Seas
slides.storyContext: Grandma traces her finger across the map: 'From Kashmir's snow peaks in the north to Kerala's backwaters in the south. From Rajasthan's golden deserts in the west to Assam's tea gardens in the east. One country, so many worlds!'
slides.inSimpleWords: India's geography is incredibly varied—mountains, deserts, forests, plains, and coastlines all make it special.

slides.title: States and Union Territories
slides.storyContext: 'How many states are there?' Ravi asks. Grandma points to different regions: 'Each state has its own capital, government, and special features.'

points.text: India has 28 states and 8 union territories.
Each state has its own capital city.
Major states include Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and West Bengal.
Union territories include Delhi, Goa, and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

slides.inSimpleWords: India is divided into states and territories, each with its own government and special identity.

slides.title: Name That Capital!
slides.storyContext: Grandma plays a game: 'Maharashtra's capital?' 'Mumbai!' Ravi shouts. 'Tamil Nadu's capital?' 'Chennai!' Priya gets it. 'West Bengal?' 'Kolkata!' They're learning India's geography through fun.
slides.inSimpleWords: Every state has a capital city that is usually its biggest and most important city.

slides.title: Languages of India
slides.storyContext: Ravi hears Grandma sing in Tamil, then speak Hindi, then English. 'How many languages does one person need to know?' Priya laughs.

points.text: India has 22 official languages recognized by the Constitution.
Hindi is spoken most widely in the north; Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam in the south.
English is widely used for business and education.
Hundreds of dialects and local languages are also spoken.

slides.inSimpleWords: India celebrates many languages—each state has its own language, yet people understand each other through respect and learning.

slides.title: Learning Languages
slides.storyContext: Grandma teaches them simple words: 'Namaste (Hindi), Vanakkam (Tamil), Namaskara (Kannada), Pranam (Bengali).' Each means 'hello' or 'respect' in different languages. 'See? One greeting, many ways to say it with love.'
slides.inSimpleWords: India's languages connect us in different ways, but respect and kindness translate to every language.

slides.title: Which Language is Spoken Where?
slides.storyContext: Grandma shows a chart: Hindi speakers in North, Tamil speakers in South, Gujarati in West, Bengali in East. 'If you travel, learn a few words in the local language. People appreciate it!'

example.problem: If 40% of Indians speak Hindi, 8% speak Bengali, 7% speak Telugu, and 6% speak Marathi, how many more people speak Hindi than all the others combined?
example.solution: Hindi speakers: 40%. Others: 8+7+6 = 21%. Difference: 40% − 21% = 19% more speak Hindi than these other languages combined.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most Indians speak Hindi, but dozens of other languages are equally important in their regions.

slides.title: Religions and Beliefs
slides.storyContext: Grandma tells them: 'Our country is home to people of many faiths. Some follow Hinduism, some Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, and Jainism. All are equal and respected.'

points.text: Hinduism is practiced by the majority of Indians.
Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, and Jainism also have millions of followers in India.
Our Constitution guarantees freedom to practice any religion.
Respect for all religions is a core value of Indian society.

slides.inSimpleWords: Indians follow many different religions, and the country respects and protects everyone's beliefs.

slides.title: Sacred Places of India
slides.storyContext: Grandma shows pictures: The golden temple in Amritsar, the Taj Mahal in Agra, the Varanasi temples by the Ganges, and the Jama Masjid in Delhi. 'Each is sacred to its followers, and all are treasured by India.'
slides.inSimpleWords: India has beautiful religious sites that show respect, architecture, and the devotion of believers.

slides.title: Indian Festivals
slides.storyContext: Ravi sees pictures of Diwali lights, Holi colors, Eid celebrations, Christmas decorations, and Durga Puja all around the room. 'We celebrate so many festivals!' he exclaims.

points.text: Diwali (Hindu Festival of Lights) brings families together with lamps and fireworks.
Holi (Festival of Colors) celebrates spring and the victory of good over evil.
Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha are celebrated by Muslims with prayers and feasts.
Christmas, Pongal, and Durga Puja are celebrated with joy and community spirit.
Each festival has its own story, traditions, and special foods.

slides.inSimpleWords: Indians celebrate different festivals throughout the year, and each festival teaches us about culture, history, and values.

slides.title: Diwali Preparations
slides.storyContext: Priya helps Grandma prepare for Diwali. They clean the house, make sweets, and buy new clothes. 'Diwali means new beginnings,' Grandma says. 'We light lamps to show that light (good) defeats darkness (evil). And we share with friends and neighbors of all religions!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Festivals in India aren't just for one religion—they're celebrated together by the whole community.

slides.title: Festival Calendar
slides.storyContext: Grandma shows a calendar: Diwali in October/November, Holi in March, Eid changes each year, Christmas in December, Pongal in January. 'We celebrate something every few weeks!'

example.problem: If Diwali is on October 31st, Holi is on March 25th, and Pongal is on January 14th, which festival comes first in the calendar year?
example.solution: Pongal (January 14th) comes first, then Holi (March 25th), then Diwali (October 31st).

slides.inSimpleWords: Indian festivals are spread throughout the year, giving us something to celebrate every season.

slides.title: People, Occupations, and Lifestyles
slides.storyContext: Grandma describes her village: 'Some people farm rice and wheat. In the cities, people work in offices, shops, hospitals, and schools. In mountains, people raise sheep and grow apples. On coasts, people fish.'

points.text: Many Indians work in farming—rice, wheat, sugar cane, and spices.
In cities, people work in offices, shops, factories, hospitals, and schools.
Coastal regions have fishing as a major occupation.
Artisans make textiles, pottery, handicrafts, and jewelry—skills passed through generations.
Different regions have different lifestyles based on geography and resources.

slides.inSimpleWords: India's people have different jobs and ways of living, but all work hard to build a strong, prosperous nation.

slides.title: A Farmer's Life
slides.storyContext: Ravi visits Uncle Raj's farm. He wakes at 5 a.m., works in the fields, and sells his rice at the market by noon. 'Farming is hard work, but I feed India,' Uncle Raj says with pride. Ravi realizes farmers are heroes.
slides.inSimpleWords: Farmers are essential to India—they grow the food we eat every day.

slides.title: Journey Across India
slides.storyContext: Grandma plans an imaginary trip: 'From Kashmir in the north with snow-capped mountains to Kerala in the south with coconut beaches. From Rajasthan's golden deserts to Assam's green tea gardens. We can travel 2,000+ kilometers and see completely different places, people, and foods.'

example.problem: If you travel from Delhi to Bangalore (about 2,150 km by road), and your car travels at 80 km per hour with a break, approximately how many hours will the journey take (not counting the break)?
example.solution: 2,150 km ÷ 80 km/hour ≈ 26.8 hours (about 27 hours of driving). With stops, a real journey takes 2-3 days.

slides.title: Tasting India's Flavors
slides.storyContext: Grandma cooks dishes from different regions: South Indian dosa, North Indian roti, Gujarati dhokla, Bengali rasogulla, and Kerala's coconut curry. 'Even our food is diverse and special!' Ravi and Priya taste the variety and love it all.
slides.inSimpleWords: Indian cuisine varies by region—each area has unique, delicious dishes based on local ingredients and traditions.

slides.title: Discover Your State
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Which state do you live in? What's special about it?'

example.problem: Research and write about your state: What is its capital? What language is spoken? What is one famous festival or feature?
example.solution: Example for Maharashtra: Capital is Mumbai. Marathi and Hindi are spoken. Diwali is a major festival, and we are known for Bollywood films, cotton farming, and the Taj Mahal (in Agra, nearby).

slides.title: Plan an Indian Adventure
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya are planning a trip across India. They want to visit a mountain region, a coastal area, a desert, and a forest. They have 30 days.

example.problem: Plan a 30-day trip visiting: Kashmir (7 days), Goa (5 days), Rajasthan (8 days), and Assam (10 days). How many days will be left for travel and rest?
example.solution: 7 + 5 + 8 + 10 = 30 days. No days left—the trip is perfectly planned! (In reality, add travel days: 7+5+8+10+4 (travel) = 34 days needed.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Planning a trip requires thinking about distances, time, and how many days you need in each place.

slides.title: Unity in Diversity Quiz
slides.storyContext: Grandma quizzes Ravi and Priya on what they've learned: 'How many states? What are major religions? Name three festivals. Which language is most spoken?'

example.problem: Answer these questions about India: (1) How many states and union territories? (2) Name 3 festivals. (3) What is the capital? (4) How many official languages?
example.solution: (1) 28 states, 8 union territories. (2) Diwali, Holi, Eid. (3) New Delhi. (4) 22 official languages.

slides.inSimpleWords: India's diversity—in languages, religions, festivals, and people—makes it one unique, beautiful country.

slides.title: India Through Their Eyes
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Ravi and Priya look at the map one more time. 'India is like a rainbow,' Priya says. 'Each color is different, but together they're beautiful.' Grandma nods: 'That's wisdom, my child. That's what makes India truly great.'
slides.inSimpleWords: India's strength comes from its diversity—each person, language, and culture adds beauty to the whole.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As evening falls, Ravi and Priya hug Grandma. They realize India is truly a land of wonders.

points.text: India is a large, democratic country with 28 states and 8 union territories.
Indians speak many languages but understand each other with respect and effort.
Multiple religions are practiced, and all are equally respected.
Festivals like Diwali, Holi, and Eid bring communities together.
People across India have different occupations and lifestyles but share pride in being Indian.
Unity in diversity is India's greatest strength.
India's geography, culture, food, and traditions make it one of the world's most vibrant nations.

slides.inSimpleWords: India is one beautiful, diverse nation where people of different religions, languages, and backgrounds live as brothers and sisters.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Visit Special Places
hook: Two friends explore India's most unique landscapes: mountains, deserts, forests, and coasts.

slides.title: Some Unique Places
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya join an educational tour with Guide Uncle to see India's most amazing landscapes.

slides.title: A Journey Through Landscapes
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle begins: 'India has the tallest mountains, vast deserts, thick forests, and beautiful coasts. Each place tells a story and is home to unique plants, animals, and people. Today, we explore these natural wonders.'

slides.title: The Himalayan Mountains
slides.storyContext: They start in the north. Guide Uncle points upward: 'The Himalayas are the tallest mountain range in the world. They stretch across northern India, protecting us like a wall.'

points.text: The Himalayas are Earth's highest mountain range, with peaks over 8,000 meters.
Mount Everest (8,849 m) is the world's tallest mountain, partly in Nepal and partly in China.
The Himalayas have rivers like the Ganga, Brahmaputra, and Indus that water the plains.
Snow leopards, musk deer, and Himalayan eagles live in these mountains.
The Himalayas give India a cool climate and are a source of water and minerals.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Himalayas are the world's tallest mountains and are home to snow, wildlife, and rushing rivers.

slides.title: Ravi's First Steps on Mountain Trails
slides.storyContext: As they trek upward, Ravi feels the air grow cooler. 'Why does the air get colder as we climb higher?' Priya asks. Guide Uncle smiles: 'The higher you go from Earth, the cooler it gets. That's why mountain peaks are frozen.'

points.text: Temperature drops about 1°C for every 100 meters you climb.
At sea level, India's heat is intense; at 3,000 meters, snow begins to appear.
This is why Himalayan towns like Shimla and Manali are cool summer retreats.

slides.title: Mountain Height Calculations
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle hands them a barometer. 'Mountains' heights are measured carefully.'

example.problem: If Mount Everest is 8,849 meters tall and the highest mountain in India, Kangchenjunga, is 8,586 meters tall, how much taller is Everest?
example.solution: 8,849 - 8,586 = 263 meters. Mount Everest is 263 meters taller than Kangchenjunga.

slides.title: The Thar Desert
slides.storyContext: They travel south and west. Suddenly, endless sand dunes stretch before them. 'Welcome to the Thar Desert,' Guide Uncle says, 'one of India's harshest environments.'

points.text: The Thar Desert covers most of Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat.
It is one of the most populated deserts in the world.
Sand dunes, very little water, and extreme heat define this landscape.
Desert plants like acacia and khejri trees survive here.
Camels, jackals, and desert foxes are adapted to live here.
People in villages farm millet and raise livestock.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Thar Desert is a vast, sandy, hot region where hardy people and animals live with little water.

slides.title: Priya Meets the Desert People
slides.storyContext: Priya meets a local family in a desert village. 'How do you survive here without water?' she asks. The farmer replies: 'We build wells, harvest rainwater, and know where underground water sleeps. The desert is harsh but home.'

points.text: Desert people are adapted to scarcity; they have centuries of knowledge.
Wells and underground water sources (aquifers) sustain villages.
Camel milk and dates are important desert foods.
Traditional clothing—turbans and loose robes—protects from sun and sand.

slides.title: Desert Survival Calculations
slides.storyContext: Ravi imagines: 'If a desert village has 50 liters of water per person per week, how much water does a family of 5 need in one month?'

example.problem: A desert family of 5 needs 50 liters per person per week. How many liters do they need per month (4 weeks)?
example.solution: Per person per month: 50 × 4 = 200 liters. For 5 people: 200 × 5 = 1,000 liters per month. A deep well must supply this.

slides.title: Tropical Forests
slides.storyContext: They move east and south, where thick green forests cover the land. 'Listen to the sounds,' Priya whispers. Birds sing, insects buzz, and water flows.

points.text: India's tropical forests cover the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, and the northeast.
These forests receive heavy rainfall and are home to thousands of species.
Tigers, elephants, leopards, and monkeys live here.
Trees produce teak, sandalwood, and many medicinal plants.
Tribal communities have lived in these forests for centuries, living in harmony with nature.

slides.inSimpleWords: Tropical forests are thick, wet jungles full of colorful animals, tall trees, and indigenous people who live sustainably.

image.alt: Tropical Forests — Some Unique Places

slides.title: Discovering Forest Medicine
slides.storyContext: A tribal guide shows them medicinal plants. 'Every leaf, every bark, every root has healing power. Our ancestors knew this for thousands of years,' she says softly.

points.text: Neem leaves cure skin ailments; ashwagandha roots reduce stress.
Turmeric and ginger grow wild in forests and are used in cooking and medicine.
Modern medicines are researched from traditional forest plants.
Protecting forests means protecting humanity's medicine cabinet.

slides.title: Forest Canopy Layers
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle explains: 'Forests have different levels, like an apartment building.'

example.problem: A rainforest has four layers: canopy (tallest trees, 30-50 m), understory (15-30 m), shrub layer (5-15 m), and forest floor (0-5 m). If one tree reaches 45 meters, which layer is its top in, and how many layers does it span from the ground?
example.solution: The top is in the canopy layer (30-50 m). The tree spans from forest floor (0 m) through all four layers to the canopy.

slides.title: Rivers of India
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle shows them a map of rivers crisscrossing India. 'Rivers are the lifelines of our country,' he says.

points.label: The Ganga
points.text: Flows from Himalayas to Bengal, worshipped and vital for millions.

points.label: The Brahmaputra
points.text: Flows through Assam, one of the largest rivers by water volume.

points.label: The Indus
points.text: Flows through Punjab and is shared with Pakistan.

points.label: The Yamuna
points.text: Joins the Ganga at Delhi.

points.label: The Godavari and Krishna
points.text: Flow through southern India.
Rivers provide water for drinking, farming, fishing, and transport.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rivers flow across India, giving water and life to millions of people and countless animals.

slides.title: Ravi's River Adventure
slides.storyContext: By the Ganga's banks, Ravi watches fishermen cast nets. 'This river feeds my family,' one fisherman says. 'But pollution hurts it now. We must protect rivers.'

points.text: Rivers are sacred in Indian culture, especially the Ganga.
Fishing communities depend entirely on river fish for income and food.
Industrial waste and sewage threaten river health.
Clean rivers mean clean water, healthy fish, and thriving communities.

slides.title: River Flow Rate Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If a river flows 1,000 cubic meters of water per second, how much water flows in one hour?'

example.problem: The Brahmaputra river flows approximately 12,000 cubic meters per second. How many cubic meters flow in one hour (3,600 seconds)?
example.solution: 12,000 × 3,600 = 43,200,000 cubic meters per hour. That's enough water to fill millions of swimming pools!

slides.title: Coasts and Beaches
slides.storyContext: They reach the Arabian Sea. Priya runs along the sandy beach. 'Oceans connect India to the world,' Guide Uncle explains.

points.text: India has a long coastline of about 7,500 kilometers.
Major coasts: Arabian Sea (west), Bay of Bengal (east), Indian Ocean (south).
Beaches like Goa, Kerala, and Kanyakumari are beautiful and attract visitors.
Fishermen catch fish, prawns, and crabs for food and livelihood.
Coral reefs and marine life thrive in shallow coastal waters.
Ports like Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata connect India to world trade.

slides.inSimpleWords: India's coasts are where the sea meets the land, bringing fish, trade, and natural beauty to Indian shores.

slides.title: The Life of a Coastal Fisherman
slides.storyContext: Priya interviews a fisherman: 'I sail every day to catch fish. The sea is beautiful but also dangerous. Monsoons close the sea for months.'

points.text: Fishing seasons are determined by monsoon winds and calm sea days.
Nets, traps, and boats are traditional fishing tools.
Coastal communities are resilient but vulnerable to storms and climate change.
Coral reef protection ensures fish populations for future generations.

slides.title: Measuring Coastline Distance
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle shows a coastal map. 'Measuring a coastline is tricky because it has so many curves.'

example.problem: India's coastline is 7,500 km. If a sailboat travels at 30 km per hour without stopping, how many days would it take to sail the entire coastline?
example.solution: 7,500 ÷ 30 = 250 hours. 250 ÷ 24 = 10.4 days (about 10-11 days of continuous sailing).

slides.title: Wetlands and Lakes
slides.storyContext: They visit a lake surrounded by birds. 'This is Chilika Lake, where migratory birds arrive each winter,' Guide Uncle points out.

points.text: Wetlands are marshy areas where water is shallow and supports rich life.
India's wetlands include lakes, marshes, and deltas.
Major lakes: Sambhar Salt Lake (Rajasthan), Loktak Lake (Manipur), Chilika Lake (Odisha).
Wetlands are homes to fish, frogs, turtles, snakes, and migratory birds.
They filter water and prevent flooding.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wetlands and lakes are wet habitats that shelter birds, fish, and plants, and help keep our water clean.

slides.title: Migratory Birds' Journey
slides.storyContext: As winter arrives, thousands of birds arrive at Chilika Lake from Siberia. Priya watches in awe: 'How do they find this place every year?'

points.text: Birds navigate using Earth's magnetic field and the sun's position.
A journey of 4,000+ km is exhausting; they need food and rest at wetlands.
If wetlands vanish, migratory birds have nowhere to rest and die.
Protecting wetlands is protecting global bird migration routes.

slides.title: Wetland Biodiversity Count
slides.storyContext: Ravi counts birds: 'If one wetland has 50 species of birds, each species has 200 birds, how many birds total?'

example.problem: Chilika Lake hosts 50 bird species. If each species has an average of 400 individuals, what is the total bird population?
example.solution: 50 × 400 = 20,000 birds. Plus thousands of fish, frogs, and reptiles. Wetlands are biodiversity hotspots!

slides.title: Comparing India's Unique Regions
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle makes a chart: 'Each region has different temperature, rainfall, height, and life.'

example.problem: The Himalayas average 5 meters of snow per year. The Thar Desert averages 0.2 meters of rain per year. How many times more snow does the Himalayas get compared to the desert's rain?
example.solution: 5 meters ÷ 0.2 meters = 25 times. The Himalayas get 25 times more precipitation than the Thar Desert.

image.alt: Comparing India's Unique Regions — Some Unique Places

slides.title: Climate and Biodiversity Connection
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle summarizes: 'Look at each region. Different climates create different plants, animals, and ways of living. This diversity is India's greatest treasure.'

points.text: Mountains = cold, snow, adaptation to altitude.
Deserts = heat, drought, water conservation.
Forests = humidity, rain, dense biodiversity.
Coasts = tides, salt, marine abundance.
Respecting every region means respecting India's natural diversity.

slides.title: Design Your Own Eco-Tour
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya are now ready: 'If you could take a tour across India, which three unique places would you visit? Why?'

example.problem: Plan a 10-day eco-tour visiting three unique Indian places. Describe what you'd see, learn, and do in each.
example.solution: Day 1-3: Himalayas (trek, see snow peaks, meet local Sherpa). Day 4-6: Goa beaches (observe marine life, relax, study fishing). Day 7-10: Western Ghats forest (wildlife safari, spot tigers and elephants, learn tribal culture).

image.alt: Design Your Own Eco-Tour — Some Unique Places

slides.title: Lessons from the Journey
slides.storyContext: As they head home, Ravi reflects: 'Every place has beauty and challenges. Protection requires understanding. This trip changed how we see India.'

points.text: Tourism brings money but also damage; eco-tourism respects the environment.
Local communities are guardians of their regions—listen to them.
Climate change threatens all unique places; each person's choices matter.
Knowledge fuels action; today's learning is tomorrow's protection.

slides.title: Human Impact on Unique Places
slides.storyContext: Guide Uncle becomes serious: 'These wonders are fragile. Human activity threatens them. We must act responsibly.'

points.text: Deforestation destroys forests and wildlife habitats.
Overfishing depletes fish populations and coral reefs.
Pollution harms rivers, lakes, and coastal ecosystems.
Plastic waste kills marine animals and poisons water.
Climate change melts glaciers and disrupts monsoons.
Everyone can help: reduce waste, protect forests, respect wildlife.

slides.inSimpleWords: Humans threaten unique places through pollution, deforestation, and overhunting. Protecting them is everyone's responsibility.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they return home with memories and photos, Ravi and Priya are amazed.

points.text: India has diverse landscapes: mountains, deserts, forests, rivers, coasts, and wetlands.
The Himalayas are the tallest mountains; the Thar is a great desert.
Tropical forests shelter incredible wildlife and indigenous communities.
Rivers and coasts are lifelines for millions of Indians.
Each unique place has its own climate, animals, plants, and people.
Respecting and protecting these places is everyone's responsibility.

slides.inSimpleWords: India's unique places—mountains, deserts, forests, rivers, and coasts—are treasures of nature that we must protect and celebrate.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Learn How Clothes are Made
hook: Two friends trace the journey of fabric from plant to wardrobe, understanding fibers, weaving, and tailoring.

slides.title: Clothes - How Things are Made
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit a textile workshop to learn where clothes come from.

slides.title: From Fiber to Fabric
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma welcomes them: 'Every piece of clothing starts as a raw material from nature. Today, I'll show you how cotton becomes your T-shirt, and how silk and wool work too.'

slides.title: Natural Fibers - Cotton
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma shows them a cotton boll—fluffy white fiber growing on a plant. 'This is cotton, India's most common cloth fiber.'

points.text: Cotton is grown from cotton plants in fields, especially in Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Telangana.
The plant produces white fluffy bolls containing seeds surrounded by cotton fiber.
Farmers harvest cotton bolls by hand or machine, then separate fiber from seeds (ginning).
Cotton is soft, breathable, and comfortable to wear in hot weather.
India is one of the world's largest cotton producers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cotton is a plant fiber that grows as fluffy white bolls; it's spun into thread to make soft, breathable clothes.

slides.title: A Farmer's Cotton Harvest
slides.storyContext: Ravi visits a cotton field. A farmer shows him: 'I plant seeds in June. By December, these white clouds are ready. One acre of cotton can make 1,000 T-shirts!'

points.text: Cotton farming requires water, sun, and rich soil.
Growth cycle is 5-7 months from seed to harvest.
Harvesting is labor-intensive; many farmers still hand-pick cotton.
One cotton plant produces 3-5 bolls, each with 15-20 grams of fiber.

slides.title: Cotton Production Mathematics
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma shows data: 'Let's calculate cotton output.'

example.problem: If one cotton plant produces 4 bolls, and one boll yields 5 grams of usable cotton fiber, how much fiber comes from 100 plants?
example.solution: Per plant: 4 bolls × 5 grams = 20 grams. For 100 plants: 20 × 100 = 2,000 grams = 2 kilograms of cotton.

slides.title: Other Natural Fibers - Wool and Silk
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma shows them samples: 'Cotton isn't the only fiber. Look at wool and silk!'

points.label: Wool
points.text: Comes from sheep and goat hair. It's warm, thick, and used for sweaters and shawls, especially in mountains.

points.label: Silk
points.text: Comes from silkworm cocoons. It's smooth, shiny, and precious. India produces silk in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

points.label: Jute
points.text: Comes from jute plants; used for bags and rugs. Grown in West Bengal.
Each fiber has unique properties suited for different types of clothes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wool comes from sheep, silk from silkworms, and jute from plants—each makes different kinds of clothes for different needs.

slides.title: The Silk Worm's Journey
slides.storyContext: Priya learns about silk production: 'A tiny silkworm spins ONE continuous thread up to 1,500 meters long! Four cocoons make just one sari.'

points.text: Silkworms are caterpillars of the silk moth.
They eat mulberry leaves for weeks, growing fast.
Then they spin their cocoon with one unbroken thread.
Harvesting silk requires carefully unwinding the cocoon thread.

slides.title: Fiber Comparison Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ravi creates a comparison: 'If one cotton plant gives 20 grams, and one silk cocoon gives 500 meters of thread, how are they different?'

example.problem: Compare: Cotton (short fibers needing spinning) vs. Silk (one long thread). If you need to make thread, which is easier? Why?
example.solution: Silk is easier—it's already one long, strong thread. Cotton requires many short fibers to be twisted together. This is why silk is more expensive and precious.

slides.title: Spinning - Fiber to Thread
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma demonstrates a spinning wheel (charkha). 'After the fiber is cleaned, we spin it into thread.'

points.text: Spinning twists loose fibers together to make strong thread.
Traditionally, a spinning wheel (charkha) is used to spin thread by hand.
Today, machines called spindles spin thread much faster in factories.
Threads are rolled onto bobbins and stored for weaving.
One cotton boll can be spun into very long, strong thread.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spinning is the process of twisting fibers together to make strong thread that can be woven into cloth.

slides.title: The Spinner's Skill
slides.storyContext: An elderly spinner shows her charkha technique. Ravi tries: 'This is hard! How do you make it so smooth?' She smiles: '50 years of practice. Your hands must feel the thread.'

points.text: Spinning requires rhythm, patience, and touch.
Too loose, the thread breaks. Too tight, it tangles.
Hand-spinners create unique, strong thread.
This craft is disappearing as machines take over.

slides.title: Thread Length Calculation
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma measures: 'Let's measure how much thread comes from spinning.'

example.problem: If spinning 100 grams of cotton fiber produces 2 kilometers of thread, how much thread comes from 500 grams?
example.solution: 500 grams ÷ 100 grams = 5 times more. 5 × 2 km = 10 kilometers of thread! That's enough for many clothes.

slides.title: Weaving - Thread to Fabric
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma leads them to a loom. 'Now we weave threads together to make fabric.'

points.text: Weaving interlaces two sets of threads: warp (vertical) and weft (horizontal).
A loom is the machine that holds and moves threads to weave them.
Traditional hand looms are still used by artisans for silk and special fabrics.
Power looms in factories weave fabric faster for mass production.
Different weave patterns create different textures: plain, twill, satin.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weaving interlaces threads together on a loom to create fabric that becomes clothes.

slides.title: The Weaver's Loom
slides.storyContext: At a hand loom, Priya watches a weaver work: 'Each pass takes care. You create patterns with your hands. This is art and craft combined.'

points.text: Hand-loom weaving is slower but produces unique, high-quality fabric.
Weavers memorize complex patterns and colors.
Indian hand-loomed cloth (sarees, dhotis) is famous worldwide.
Machine weaving is fast but produces standard, repetitive patterns.

slides.title: Weaving Speed Comparison
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: 'How long would it take to weave one sari by hand vs. machine?'

example.problem: A hand loom weaves 50 centimeters of fabric per hour. A power loom weaves 500 centimeters per hour. A sari needs 6 meters (600 cm) of fabric. How long for each method?
example.solution: Hand loom: 600 ÷ 50 = 12 hours. Power loom: 600 ÷ 500 = 1.2 hours (just over 1 hour). Hand-looming is 10 times slower!

slides.title: Dyeing - Adding Color
slides.storyContext: Priya sees big vats of colored water. 'How does cloth get its color?' Mrs. Sharma smiles: 'Dyes!'

points.text: After weaving, white fabric is dyed to add color.
Dyes are mixed into hot water, and fabric is soaked and stirred.
Traditional dyes came from plants (indigo for blue, madder for red, turmeric for yellow).
Modern synthetic dyes give bright, long-lasting colors.
Dyeing must be done carefully to avoid pollution of waterways.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dyeing soaks fabric in colored water to give it the colors we see in our clothes.

slides.title: The Indigo Tradition
slides.storyContext: An old dyer explains: 'Indigo is sacred in India. For centuries, we've dyed with this plant. It creates the deepest blue.'

points.text: Indigo is extracted from the indigo plant leaves.
The dyeing process requires special fermentation techniques.
Indigo dye gets deeper with repeated dipping and sun exposure.
Hand-dyed indigo cloth is more expensive and eco-friendly than synthetic dyes.

slides.title: Dye Batch Calculations
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma teaches: 'Dye calculations ensure consistent color.'

example.problem: One liter of dye concentrate can color 10 meters of fabric. If you need to dye 50 meters of fabric evenly, how much dye concentrate do you need?
example.solution: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 liters of dye concentrate needed. Then it's mixed with 50 liters of water for even coloring.

slides.title: Finishing and Tailoring
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma shows finished fabric rolls and a tailor's shop. 'Now the final steps!'

points.text: Fabric is finished: pressed, softened, and treated for comfort.
Large rolls of fabric are sent to tailors or garment factories.
Patterns are cut from fabric; pieces are stitched together with a sewing machine.
A single shirt or dress needs multiple pieces cut and sewn precisely.
Quality checks ensure seams are strong and clothes fit well.
Then clothes are packaged and sent to shops for sale.

slides.inSimpleWords: Finished fabric is cut into pieces and stitched together by tailors to make the shirts, pants, and dresses we wear.

slides.title: At the Tailor's Shop
slides.storyContext: Ravi watches a master tailor work: 'Cutting is the secret. One mistake ruins meters of fabric. A curved scissors, steady hands, experience—that's the skill.'

points.text: Tailors must understand how to cut patterns economically.
Skilled tailors waste less fabric and create better-fitting clothes.
Custom tailoring is more expensive but perfectly fitted.
Factory tailoring is fast but one-size-fits-most.

slides.title: Fabric Cutting and Waste
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates: 'If cutting patterns wastes fabric, how much is wasted?'

example.problem: A tailor uses 2 meters of fabric to cut one shirt. The waste is 0.3 meters. If the tailor makes 100 shirts, how much total fabric is used, and how much is wasted?
example.solution: Total fabric used: 2 × 100 = 200 meters. Total waste: 0.3 × 100 = 30 meters. Waste is 30 ÷ 200 = 15% of total fabric.

slides.title: The Journey of a Cotton T-Shirt
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma traces the complete path: 'Your T-shirt traveled many steps before reaching your wardrobe!'

example.problem: A cotton T-shirt takes: 1 week to grow cotton, 2 days to gin and clean fiber, 3 days to spin thread, 2 days to weave fabric, 1 day to dye, 1 day to finish, 5 days to cut and sew, and 3 days for packaging and shipping. How many days total does it take?
example.solution: 7 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 5 + 3 = 24 days. A T-shirt takes about 3-4 weeks from field to closet!

image.alt: The Journey of a Cotton T-Shirt — Clothes - How Things are Made

slides.title: Workers Behind Our Clothes
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma becomes reflective: 'Behind every piece of clothing, there are farmers, spinners, weavers, dyers, and tailors. Many are paid very little. Fair wages matter.'

points.text: Textile workers are often underpaid and overworked.
Child labor is still used in some countries' garment factories.
Fair trade certification ensures ethical wages and conditions.
Buying ethically-made clothes supports good working conditions.

slides.title: Synthetic Fibers - Modern Alternatives
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma shows synthetic fibers: 'Polyester, nylon, and acrylic are human-made. They're cheaper but not always better.'

points.text: Synthetic fibers are made from petroleum (oil).
They're durable, colorfast, and quick-drying.
But they don't breathe like cotton and harm the environment when washed.
Microplastics from synthetic fibers end up in oceans.
Natural fibers are biodegradable and often better for health.

slides.inSimpleWords: Synthetic fibers like polyester are cheap and durable but are made from oil and damage the environment.

slides.title: Design and Calculate Cloth
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya try: 'Can we design and estimate materials?'

example.problem: You want to make a simple kurta. The pattern requires 1.5 meters of fabric for the body, 0.5 meters for sleeves, and 0.2 meters for the collar. How much fabric do you need in total? If fabric costs 200 rupees per meter, what's the total cost?
example.solution: Total fabric: 1.5 + 0.5 + 0.2 = 2.2 meters. Cost: 2.2 × 200 = 440 rupees.

slides.title: The Global Textile Trade
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma shows them labels: 'Made in Bangladesh, Made in Vietnam, Made in India. Textiles travel the world, but so do the workers' stories.'

points.text: India's textile industry is one of the oldest in the world.
But today, competition comes from cheaper countries like Bangladesh and Vietnam.
Indian hand-looms and silk are still prized for quality and tradition.
Supporting Indian textiles means supporting millions of skilled workers.

slides.title: Sustainability in Fashion
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma teaches: 'Fast fashion wastes fabric, water, and money. Sustainable fashion is better.'

points.text: Fast fashion means making cheap clothes quickly, creating massive waste.
Cotton farming uses pesticides that harm soil and water.
Dyeing produces pollution if not done carefully.
Sustainable fashion: buy less, choose quality, repair instead of discarding.
Natural fibers and ethical production protect the environment.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sustainable fashion means caring for the environment and workers by buying ethical, quality clothes that last.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they leave the workshop wearing their learning proudly, Ravi and Priya now know the story behind every cloth.

points.text: Clothes come from natural fibers: cotton, wool, silk, and jute.
Fibers are spun into thread on spinning wheels or machines.
Threads are woven together on looms to make fabric.
Fabric is dyed, finished, and tailored into clothes.
Many steps and many workers are involved in making each piece of clothing.
Understanding this journey helps us respect clothes and buy mindfully.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every piece of clothing is the result of many steps—from growing fiber to spinning, weaving, dyeing, and tailoring—and involves many skilled workers.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Discover Nature's Cycles
hook: Two friends explore the seasons, weather patterns, day-night cycles, and how nature changes throughout the year.

slides.title: Rhythms of Nature
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya notice that nature changes with seasons and time. They ask their Dad to explain.

slides.title: Nature's Time Clock
slides.storyContext: Dad shows them his weather journal: 'Every day, every season, nature follows patterns. The sun rises and sets. Rains come and go. Plants grow and rest. This is the rhythm of nature.'

slides.title: Day and Night - A Daily Cycle
slides.storyContext: Dad points out the window: 'Right now, children in Australia are sleeping because it's night there, while we have the sun.'

points.text: Earth rotates (spins) on its axis every 24 hours.
Day happens when your part of Earth faces the sun; night when it faces away.
Day lasts about 12 hours; night about 12 hours.
Different parts of Earth have day and night at different times simultaneously.
The sun doesn't actually move; Earth's rotation creates the illusion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth spins, causing day (when the sun is above us) and night (when the sun is on the other side of Earth) in a 24-hour cycle.

image.alt: Day and Night - A Daily Cycle — Rhythms of Nature

slides.title: Sunrise and Sunset Patterns
slides.storyContext: Priya notices: 'In summer, sunrise is early. In winter, it's late. Why?' Dad explains: 'Earth's tilt changes how long daylight lasts.'

points.text: Sunrise and sunset times change throughout the year.
In summer (June), sunrise is around 5:30 a.m.; in winter (December), around 7:30 a.m.
Summer has longer days (up to 15 hours of daylight) and shorter nights.
Winter has shorter days (9 hours of daylight) and longer nights.
This happens because Earth's axis tilts toward or away from the sun.

slides.title: Daylight Hours Calculation
slides.storyContext: Dad shows a data table: 'Let's calculate daylight duration.'

example.problem: In Delhi, June has 15 hours of daylight and December has 9 hours. How many more hours of daylight are there in June than December?
example.solution: 15 - 9 = 6 extra hours in June. Summer days are 6 hours longer than winter days!

slides.title: The Seasons
slides.storyContext: Dad shows a diagram: 'Earth also tilts and orbits the sun, creating four seasons.'

points.label: Summer
points.text: Sun is high, days are long, weather is hot. In India (Northern Hemisphere): March-May.

points.label: Monsoon (Rainy Season)
points.text: Winds bring heavy rains. In India: June-September. Rivers swell, fields are flooded for farming.

points.label: Autumn
points.text: Temperature drops, skies clear, leaves fall in some places. In India: October-November.

points.label: Winter
points.text: Sun is low, days are short, weather is cool/cold. In India (Northern Hemisphere): December-February.
Seasons repeat every year in the same order.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's tilt creates four seasons—summer, monsoon, autumn, and winter—each with different weather and activities.

slides.title: The Monsoon Arrives
slides.storyContext: Ravi watches the sky darken: 'Dad, is the monsoon coming?' Suddenly, thunder roars. Rain pours. Priya cheers: 'Look! All of India is waiting for these rains!'

points.text: Monsoon rains are essential for farming in India.
Farmers pray for monsoon onset because crops depend on it.
If monsoon rains are delayed, crops fail and famine threatens.
If monsoon rains are too heavy, floods destroy everything.

slides.title: The Monsoon - India's Life-Giving Rains
slides.storyContext: Priya looks excited: 'The monsoon is so important to India!' Dad nods: 'It's the most crucial season for farming and water.'

points.text: The monsoon is the season of heavy rainfall from June to September.
Wind patterns shift, bringing moisture from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.
Farmers rely on monsoon rains to grow rice, wheat, and other crops.
Rivers and dams fill up during monsoons, storing water for dry seasons.
Floods can happen if monsoon rains are too heavy; droughts if rains fail.
Wildlife depends on monsoon rains to find water and food.

slides.inSimpleWords: The monsoon brings heavy rains that fill rivers, water crops, and sustain all life in India for the entire year.

image.alt: The Monsoon - India's Life-Giving Rains — Rhythms of Nature

slides.title: Monsoon Rainfall Analysis
slides.storyContext: Ravi collects rain data: 'If the monsoon brings 80 cm of rain in 4 months, how much rain per month?'

example.problem: India's monsoon brings 800 mm (80 cm) of rain over June-September (4 months). What is the average monthly rainfall?
example.solution: 80 cm ÷ 4 months = 20 cm per month during monsoon. Compare this to 5 cm in winter—monsoon brings 4 times more rain!

slides.title: Weather and Climate
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: 'What's the difference between weather and climate, Dad?' Dad explains clearly.

points.label: Weather
points.text: The condition of the atmosphere on a particular day: sunny, rainy, hot, cold. It can change quickly.

points.label: Climate
points.text: The average weather pattern of a place over many years. It changes slowly.
India has a tropical climate with hot summers, monsoon rains, and mild winters.
Mountains have a temperate/cold climate; deserts are hot and dry year-round.
Climate affects what crops grow, what animals live, and how people dress.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weather is what happens today (rainy, sunny); climate is the long-term pattern of weather a region experiences.

slides.title: Weather vs. Climate Story
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If it snows in Kashmir in winter, is India a cold country?' Dad smiles: 'No. One snowy day is weather. India's 30-year pattern is tropical climate.'

points.text: One rainy day doesn't mean your town is wet; climate is a 30-year average.
Weather stations record temperature, rainfall, and wind every day.
Climate data comes from decades of weather records.
Understanding climate helps predict long-term trends and plan agriculture.

slides.title: Weather Data Over Time
slides.storyContext: Dad shows Ravi weather records: 'Let's see how weather varies even in the same month.'

example.problem: Delhi's daily temperatures in June: Day 1: 38°C, Day 2: 35°C, Day 3: 40°C, Day 4: 37°C. What is the average temperature for these 4 days?
example.solution: (38 + 35 + 40 + 37) ÷ 4 = 150 ÷ 4 = 37.5°C average. Days vary, but the average shows the climate trend.

slides.title: Water Cycle - Nature's Recycling
slides.storyContext: Dad fills a glass with water. 'This water has been on Earth for billions of years, recycling endlessly.'

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Heat from the sun turns water from oceans, rivers, and lakes into water vapor (invisible gas).

points.label: Condensation
points.text: Water vapor cools in the upper atmosphere and forms tiny water droplets—creating clouds.

points.label: Precipitation
points.text: Clouds become heavy and release water as rain, snow, or hail.

points.label: Collection
points.text: Water flows into rivers and oceans, and the cycle begins again.
This cycle ensures fresh water is constantly recycled to land and organisms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water evaporates from oceans, forms clouds, falls as rain, and returns to oceans—an endless natural cycle.

slides.title: Tracing a Water Droplet
slides.storyContext: Dad imagines: 'This water in your glass was once part of the Indian Ocean. It evaporated, fell as rain, ran into a river, and ended up here. Tomorrow, it might evaporate again.'

points.text: Water molecules move continuously through the environment.
A droplet might spend years in the ocean, days in clouds, or minutes in plants.
Transpiration—water from plants—adds water to the atmosphere too.
This cycle has recycled water for 3.5 billion years.

slides.title: Evaporation and Condensation Calculation
slides.storyContext: Priya conducts an experiment: 'If a puddle evaporates 50% of its water in one day, how much remains?'

example.problem: A puddle holds 1 liter of water. On a hot, sunny day, 50% evaporates. The remaining water is collected. On day 2, 50% of the remaining water evaporates. How much is left after 2 days?
example.solution: After Day 1: 1 liter × 50% = 0.5 liters remain. After Day 2: 0.5 × 50% = 0.25 liters remain.

slides.title: Seasons Affect Plants and Animals
slides.storyContext: Priya observes: 'In summer, mango trees fruit. In winter, mustard blooms. Animals behave differently too.'

points.text: Plants bloom, fruit, and rest according to seasons.
Spring brings new leaves and flowers; monsoon brings lush green growth.
Autumn sees seeds disperse; winter sees dormancy (plants rest).
Animals migrate during seasons (birds flying south in winter).
Hibernation and breeding are timed to seasonal availability of food.
Humans plant crops and harvest according to seasonal rhythms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants flower, fruit, and rest in different seasons; animals migrate, hibernate, or breed according to seasonal changes.

slides.title: Migration Mysteries
slides.storyContext: Ravi wonders: 'Birds fly thousands of kilometers every season. How do they know where to go?' Dad says: 'They follow ancient paths, guided by sun and Earth's magnetic field.'

points.text: Migratory birds follow the same routes every year, sometimes for millions of years of evolution.
Arctic terns migrate 44,000 km annually—the longest migration on Earth.
Birds navigate using the sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, and landmarks.
Climate change disrupts migration timing, threatening bird populations.

slides.title: Bird Migration Distance
slides.storyContext: Ravi calculates: 'If a bird migrates 8,000 km twice yearly (there and back), how far in 10 years?'

example.problem: An Arctic tern migrates 22,000 km one way. It travels there and back each year. In 20 years, how far total does it fly?
example.solution: Per year: 22,000 × 2 = 44,000 km. In 20 years: 44,000 × 20 = 880,000 km! More than Earth's circumference.

slides.title: Temperature Changes Through Seasons
slides.storyContext: Dad shows a graph: 'Here's Delhi's average temperature for each month. See the pattern?'

example.problem: Delhi's average temperatures: Jan 12°C, Feb 15°C, Mar 25°C, Apr 32°C, May 35°C, Jun 32°C, Jul 29°C, Aug 28°C, Sep 28°C, Oct 25°C, Nov 18°C, Dec 13°C. What is the highest temperature month? The lowest?
example.solution: Highest: May at 35°C (peak summer). Lowest: January at 12°C (peak winter). The difference is 23°C. Summer is much hotter than winter in Delhi.

slides.title: Climate Change and Seasonal Shifts
slides.storyContext: Dad becomes serious: 'I've kept this journal for 30 years. Monsoons are arriving later. Summers are hotter. Winters are shorter. This is climate change.'

points.text: Global temperatures are rising due to greenhouse gases.
Monsoon timing is becoming unpredictable, threatening harvests.
Heat waves are more frequent and intense.
Glaciers in the Himalayas are melting, threatening river water supplies.
Every person's choices (energy use, car trips, waste) affect global climate.

slides.title: Track Nature's Rhythms
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya decide: 'Let's observe and record for one year!'

example.problem: Keep a nature journal for 12 months. Record: daily sunrise/sunset time (changes with seasons), monthly rainfall, monthly temperature highs/lows, when trees flower or fruit, when birds arrive/depart, and when you need different clothes. What patterns do you notice?
example.solution: Expected findings: Sunrise is earliest in summer (5:30 a.m.) and latest in winter (7:30 a.m.). Monsoon (Jun-Sep) has highest rainfall. Temperature peaks in May-June. Most animals breed in spring.

slides.title: Lunar Cycles - The Moon's Rhythms
slides.storyContext: Dad points at the moon: 'The moon also has a rhythm. It orbits Earth every 29.5 days, changing shape as it orbits.'

points.text: New moon: invisible (sun-facing side faces Earth).
Waxing crescent/gibbous: moon grows larger in the night sky.
Full moon: fully lit side faces Earth, at its brightest.
Waning crescent/gibbous: moon shrinks until new moon again.
The moon influences ocean tides and affects ocean life.

slides.inSimpleWords: The moon orbits Earth, cycling through phases—new, crescent, half, full—every 29.5 days, affecting tides and life.

slides.title: Tides and the Moon
slides.storyContext: At the beach, Priya notices: 'The water goes up and down twice a day. What moves it?' Dad explains: 'The moon's gravity pulls Earth's oceans.'

points.text: The moon's gravity creates tides—high tide when the moon is overhead, low tide on the opposite side.
Tides follow the lunar cycle; high tide occurs every 12 hours 25 minutes.
Coastal creatures time their life cycles (breeding, feeding) to tides.
Humans use tidal energy to generate electricity.

slides.title: Tidal Cycle Calculation
slides.storyContext: Ravi learns: 'If tides occur every 12.4 hours, how many high tides in one month?'

example.problem: High tide occurs every 12 hours 25 minutes. In one 30-day month (720 hours), how many high tides occur?
example.solution: 12.4 hours per tide cycle. 720 ÷ 12.4 ≈ 58 high tides per month. Twice daily for 30 days = ~60 tides.

slides.title: Predicting Nature's Patterns
slides.storyContext: Dad reflects: 'By understanding rhythms, we predict and prepare. Farmers know when to sow. Fishermen know when tides are right. Predictions save lives.'

points.text: Weather forecasting uses patterns to warn of storms and prepare people.
Climate science predicts long-term trends to plan cities and agriculture.
Understanding seasonal rhythms helps doctors predict disease outbreaks.
Every prediction starts with understanding nature's cycles.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they close their nature journals, Ravi and Priya feel connected to the natural world.

points.text: Earth's rotation creates a 24-hour day-night cycle.
Earth's tilt creates four seasons: summer, monsoon, autumn, and winter.
The monsoon is India's most important season, bringing life-giving rains.
Weather changes daily; climate is a long-term pattern.
The water cycle recycles water endlessly: evaporation, condensation, precipitation.
Plants and animals follow nature's seasonal rhythms for survival and reproduction.
Understanding nature's rhythms helps us live in harmony with our environment.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nature follows rhythms—day and night, seasons, water cycles—that shape weather, seasons, plants, animals, and human life.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Protect Our Planet
hook: Two friends learn how Earth supports all life and explore ways to protect it for future generations.

slides.title: Earth - Our Shared Home
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit an environmental center with Eco Uncle to learn about protecting our planet.

image.alt: Earth - Our Shared Home — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: One Planet, Many Lives
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle begins: 'Earth is our shared home. It sustains 8 billion humans and millions of animal and plant species. Today, we learn how to care for it.'

slides.title: Earth's Structure and Resources
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows a globe with layers: 'Earth has a solid crust, liquid interior, and atmosphere. Each provides resources we need.'

points.text: The crust is Earth's solid outer layer with soil, minerals, and rocks.
Beneath the crust is the mantle and core, generating Earth's heat.
Oceans cover 71% of Earth; land covers 29%.
The atmosphere (air) protects us from harmful sun rays and keeps us warm.
Soil, water, forests, minerals, and fossil fuels are Earth's natural resources.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is layered like an onion, with a crust, mantle, and core, surrounded by an atmosphere that protects all life.

slides.title: Priya's Discovery at the Aquarium
slides.storyContext: Priya watches fish swimming and says, 'Every creature depends on this water. If the ocean gets polluted, these animals die.' Eco Uncle nods: 'That's why we must protect every corner of Earth.'

points.text: Water covers most of Earth and is home to millions of species.
Oceans regulate climate and produce oxygen.

slides.title: Biodiversity - The Web of Life
slides.storyContext: Priya looks at pictures of rainforests, coral reefs, and grasslands. 'So many different creatures! They're all connected,' she says.
