points.text: Biodiversity means the variety of all living organisms and ecosystems on Earth.
Over 8 million species of animals, plants, fungi, and microbes exist.
Each species plays a role: plants produce oxygen, pollinators spread seeds, predators control pests.
Ecosystems are communities of organisms and their environment, interdependent.
Rainforests, grasslands, deserts, oceans, and wetlands each have unique biodiversity.
Loss of one species can affect the whole ecosystem.

slides.inSimpleWords: Biodiversity is the incredible variety of life—millions of species—all connected in webs where each plays an important role.

slides.title: Food Chains: Who Eats What?
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws a food chain: 'Grass is eaten by rabbits, and rabbits are eaten by eagles. If grass dies, rabbits starve, and eagles starve too!'

example.problem: In a grassland ecosystem, if all the flowers die, what happens to the bees and birds that eat the flowers?
example.solution: Bees and birds lose their food source and must move elsewhere or starve. The ecosystem breaks down.

slides.title: Environmental Problems
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows photos of pollution, deforestation, and climate change. 'These problems threaten our home,' he says gravely.

points.label: Air Pollution
points.text: Smoke from factories, vehicles, and burning waste makes air toxic, causing health problems.

points.label: Water Pollution
points.text: Chemicals, plastic waste, and sewage contaminate rivers and oceans, harming aquatic life.

points.label: Soil Pollution
points.text: Pesticides and industrial waste make soil unhealthy, reducing crop yield.

points.label: Deforestation
points.text: Cutting forests for timber and farmland destroys habitats and reduces oxygen production.

points.label: Climate Change
points.text: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂, trapping heat and warming Earth, causing extreme weather.

points.label: Plastic Waste
points.text: Plastic lasts hundreds of years, choking oceans and harming wildlife.

slides.inSimpleWords: Our planet faces serious problems: air, water, and soil pollution; loss of forests; rising temperatures; and mountains of plastic waste.

slides.title: Ravi Sees Pollution in His City
slides.storyContext: Ravi looks at the smoggy sky over the city and coughs. 'Why is the air so bad?' he asks. Eco Uncle explains: 'Car exhaust, factory smoke, and burning waste create smog. It makes us sick and harms plants too.'

points.text: Smog reduces visibility and harms lungs.
Polluted air weakens trees and crops.

slides.title: Conservation and Sustainable Living
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle smiles: 'But we can fix these problems! It starts with us making smart choices.'

points.label: Reduce
points.text: Use less. Buy only what you need. Avoid single-use plastics.

points.label: Reuse
points.text: Use things again: old clothes as rags, glass jars as containers, paper bags instead of plastic.

points.label: Recycle
points.text: Separate waste: paper, plastic, metal, glass. Factories turn recycled materials into new products.

points.label: Plant Trees
points.text: Trees clean air, provide shade, and give homes to animals.

points.label: Save Water
points.text: Turn off taps, take short showers, fix leaks, use rainwater harvesting.

points.label: Save Energy
points.text: Use LED bulbs, turn off lights, avoid air conditioning when possible.

slides.inSimpleWords: We can protect Earth by reducing waste, reusing items, recycling, planting trees, and saving water and energy.

slides.title: Priya's Zero-Waste Lunch Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya brings lunch in a steel container and glass bottle instead of plastic bags. 'No trash!' she announces proudly. Ravi tries it too and saves 5 plastic bags per week.

example.problem: If one child reduces plastic waste by 5 bags per week, and there are 100 children in a school doing this, how many plastic bags are saved per week? Per year?
example.solution: Per week: 100 × 5 = 500 bags. Per year: 500 × 52 = 26,000 bags saved! One school prevents 26,000 bags from polluting our oceans.

slides.title: Renewable Energy - Clean Power
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows solar panels on the roof. 'Energy from the sun, wind, and water are clean and endless.'

points.label: Solar Energy
points.text: Panels convert sunlight into electricity. No pollution, lasts millions of years.

points.label: Wind Energy
points.text: Wind turbines use wind to generate electricity. Common in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.

points.label: Hydroelectric Energy
points.text: Dams use flowing water to produce electricity without burning fossil fuels.

points.label: Biogas
points.text: Farm waste and cow dung are converted to cooking gas, reducing waste.
Renewable energy replaces coal, oil, and natural gas, stopping greenhouse gas emissions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Renewable energy from the sun, wind, and water powers homes without pollution and lasts forever.

image.alt: Renewable Energy - Clean Power — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: Visit to a Solar Village
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit a village powered entirely by solar energy. Every house has panels, and the village has no pollution. 'This is the future!' says Priya excitedly.

points.text: Solar villages prove renewable energy works at scale.
Communities can be fully powered by clean energy.

slides.title: Comparing Energy Sources
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle compares: 'Coal plants produce electricity but emit 1 ton of CO₂ per megawatt. Solar produces zero emissions.'

example.problem: If a coal plant produces 1,000 tons of CO₂ per day and a solar plant produces 0 tons, how much CO₂ does coal produce in a year compared to solar?
example.solution: Coal: 1,000 × 365 = 365,000 tons CO₂ per year. Solar: 0 tons. Coal produces 365,000 more tons of harmful emissions annually.

slides.title: Global Cooperation for Earth
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: 'Can one country fix Earth's problems alone?' Eco Uncle shakes his head: 'No, the whole world must work together.'

points.text: The United Nations brings countries together to protect the environment.
Paris Climate Agreement: Nations pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Protected areas and national parks preserve biodiversity.
International laws ban harmful chemicals and regulate whaling and poaching.
NGOs (non-governmental organizations) work globally on environmental issues.
Young activists push governments to act faster on climate change.

slides.inSimpleWords: Countries, organizations, and people worldwide must work together to protect oceans, forests, atmosphere, and wildlife.

image.alt: Global Cooperation for Earth — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: India's Role in Climate Action
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shares: 'India has committed to planting 70 billion trees and shifting to 50% renewable energy by 2030. Every Indian can help!'

points.text: India is a global leader in renewable energy expansion.
Youth movements in India push for stronger climate policies.

slides.title: Carbon Footprint Calculation
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle teaches them: 'Every activity releases carbon dioxide. This is your carbon footprint.'

example.problem: Ravi's family activities per day: car drive = 2 kg CO₂, electricity use = 1.5 kg CO₂, food = 1 kg CO₂, waste = 0.5 kg CO₂. What is their daily carbon footprint? Weekly?
example.solution: Daily: 2 + 1.5 + 1 + 0.5 = 5 kg CO₂. Weekly: 5 × 7 = 35 kg CO₂. They can reduce by using public transport, saving electricity, eating less meat, and reducing waste.

slides.title: Personal Environmental Footprint
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates her family's footprint and realizes even small changes add up: 'If I walk instead of taking a car 3 times a week, I save 6 kg of CO₂!'

points.label: Food Footprint
points.text: Meat production uses more water and land than vegetables.

points.label: Transport Footprint
points.text: Cars emit CO₂; public transport and walking are cleaner.

points.label: Energy Footprint
points.text: Electricity from coal is dirtier than solar or wind.

points.label: Waste Footprint
points.text: Recycling reduces the energy needed to make new products.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gases your activities produce. Small changes in daily habits reduce it significantly.

slides.title: Ravi and Priya's School Project Proposal
slides.storyContext: At school, Ravi and Priya present their eco-project idea to the principal: a school garden using compost, rainwater harvesting, and solar lights to power everything.

points.text: Students can lead environmental projects at school.
Small school projects inspire whole communities.

slides.title: Design Your Eco-Project
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya are inspired: 'What can we do at home or school to help Earth?'

example.problem: Design a project to reduce waste, save water, or plant trees at your home or school. What will you do? How many people will participate? What is your goal?
example.solution: Example: Start a composting program at school. Collect vegetable waste from the cafeteria, compost it in the garden for 3 months, and use the compost to grow vegetables. Goal: reduce waste by 50% and grow 20 kg of organic vegetables for the school kitchen.

slides.title: Circular Economy: Waste to Treasure
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle explains: 'In a circular economy, waste from one process becomes input for another. Nothing is truly wasted.'

points.label: Old Clothes
points.text: Donated clothes are reused; worn ones become rags or insulation.

points.label: Plastic Waste
points.text: Recycled plastic becomes benches, bags, or construction materials.

points.label: Food Waste
points.text: Composted food scraps grow new vegetables and plants.

points.label: Paper
points.text: Shredded paper becomes packaging or cardboard.

slides.inSimpleWords: A circular economy recycles waste into new useful products, protecting resources and reducing pollution.

slides.title: From Plastic Bottles to Park Benches
slides.storyContext: Priya visits a recycling center and sees plastic bottles being shredded and molded into park benches. '1,000 bottles make one bench!' says the worker.

example.problem: If each park bench requires 1,000 plastic bottles and a park has 20 benches, how many bottles were recycled? If an average person uses 52 bottles per year, how many people's annual waste makes these benches?
example.solution: Bottles for benches: 20 × 1,000 = 20,000 bottles. People's annual waste: 20,000 ÷ 52 ≈ 385 people's yearly bottles used in just one park.

slides.title: Protecting Earth's Ecosystems
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle highlights critical ecosystems: 'Rainforests, coral reefs, and wetlands are Earth's lungs. We must protect them completely.'

points.label: Rainforests
points.text: Produce 20% of Earth's oxygen; home to 50% of all species; regulate rainfall.

points.label: Coral Reefs
points.text: Support 25% of ocean life; protect coastlines from storms; provide food and medicine.

points.label: Wetlands
points.text: Filter water; prevent floods; provide homes for birds and fish.

points.label: Forests
points.text: Store carbon, prevent erosion, and sustain millions of lives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's critical ecosystems like rainforests, reefs, and wetlands must be protected because they sustain all life.

slides.title: Visiting a Protected Forest Reserve
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya trek through a protected rainforest. They spot rare birds, jaguars, and undiscovered plants. 'This is why we must protect forests!' says Priya in wonder.

points.text: Protected areas preserve biodiversity and wildlife habitats.
Ecotourism provides income for local communities to conserve forests.

slides.title: Mangrove Forests and Coastal Protection
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle explains: 'Mangroves are special trees that grow in water. They protect coastlines from storms and provide homes for fish, crabs, and birds.'

example.problem: A coastal area with 100 hectares of mangrove forest is protected. Each hectare provides habitat for 500 species. If mangroves are cut down, how many species lose their homes?
example.solution: Total species: 100 × 500 = 50,000 species would lose homes if all mangroves are destroyed. This is why protection is critical.

slides.title: The Friends Make a Promise
slides.storyContext: As the day ends, Ravi and Priya make a promise to Eco Uncle: 'We will use less, plant trees, save water and energy, and inspire others to protect Earth.'

points.text: Individual actions create collective change.
Young people can be environmental leaders.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they leave the environmental center, Ravi and Priya feel empowered and hopeful.

points.text: Earth is our shared home with incredible biodiversity and natural resources.
Environmental problems—pollution, deforestation, climate change—threaten all life.
The 3 R's (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) and conservation actions can protect Earth.
Renewable energy from sun, wind, and water replaces dirty fossil fuels.
Global cooperation is essential: countries, organizations, and individuals must work together.
Young people like Ravi and Priya are the future guardians of Earth.
Small actions by millions of people can create big, positive change.
A circular economy reduces waste and protects Earth's limited resources.
Protecting critical ecosystems like rainforests and coral reefs sustains all life on Earth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is our only home, and protecting it is everyone's responsibility. By reducing waste, saving resources, and acting together, we can create a healthy planet for future generations.

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Sweet Cake Adventure
hook: Two friends divide a birthday cake and discover the magic of fractions.

slides.title: Fractions: Parts of a Whole
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi discover the magic of fractions through cakes, ribbons, and everyday objects.

image.alt: Fractions: Parts of a Whole — Fractions

slides.title: The Birthday Cake Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother baked a big round cake. She asked Anaya and Ravi to divide it fairly among their 4 friends. Anaya cut the cake into 4 equal pieces.

points.label: Setup
points.text: One whole cake divided into 4 equal parts

slides.inSimpleWords: One cake cut into 4 equal pieces makes fractions.

slides.title: Understanding Numerator and Denominator
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at one slice. 'That's 1 out of 4 pieces,' he said. Anaya wrote: 1/4.

points.label: Numerator
points.text: The number on top (1) = how many pieces we take

points.label: Denominator
points.text: The number below (4) = total equal pieces

points.label: Fraction
points.text: 1/4 means one part out of four

points.label: Read It
points.text: 1/4 is read as 'one-fourth' or 'one-quarter'

slides.inSimpleWords: Top number = pieces taken. Bottom number = total pieces.

slides.title: Sharing Among Friends
slides.storyContext: When Ravi takes 1 slice, he has 1/4 of the cake. When Anaya takes 2 slices, she has 2/4. Their friend Tina takes 1 slice, and Ravi's brother takes the last slice.

points.text: 4/4 means all four pieces, which is the complete cake.

slides.title: Fractions as Division
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother says: 'Cutting the cake into equal parts is like dividing. 1/4 means divide 1 cake by 4 people.'

points.label: Division
points.text: A fraction is a way to show division: a ÷ b = a/b

points.label: One Cake, 4 People
points.text: 1 ÷ 4 = 1/4 (each person gets one-fourth)

points.label: One Pizza, 8 Slices
points.text: 1 ÷ 8 = 1/8 (each slice is one-eighth)

points.label: Fair Share
points.text: Fractions help divide things equally among people.

slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction shows how to divide one thing into equal parts and share them fairly.

slides.title: Working with Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya took 2 slices for herself and Ravi. That was 2/4 of the cake.

example.problem: If Anaya eats 2 slices out of 4, what fraction is that?
example.solution: 2 slices taken ÷ 4 total slices = 2/4 (which simplifies to 1/2)

points.label: Remember
points.text: Multiple parts of the same fraction add together

slides.inSimpleWords: Two slices out of four is 2/4 or half the cake.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mother cut another identical cake into 8 pieces. Ravi took 4 slices from this cake. 'Look, Anaya! I have the same amount as you!' he said.

points.label: Same Amount
points.text: 2/4 from first cake = 4/8 from second cake

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Different fractions, same value

points.label: Multiply
points.text: 2/4 × 2/2 = 4/8 (multiply top and bottom by same number)

points.label: Divide
points.text: 4/8 ÷ 2/2 = 2/4 (divide top and bottom by same number)

slides.inSimpleWords: Half a cake = 2/4 = 4/8. Different numbers, same part.

image.alt: Understanding Numerator and Denominator — Fractions

slides.title: The Ribbon Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya has a ribbon and cuts it into 3 equal pieces. She gives Ravi 1 piece (1/3) and keeps 2 pieces for herself (2/3). 'Look, I have twice as much as you!' laughs Anaya.

points.text: 1/3 + 2/3 = 3/3 = 1 whole ribbon
2/3 is twice as much as 1/3

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: At the party, Anaya's friend got 1/2 of a chocolate bar, and another friend got 2/4 of an identical bar. 'They're the same!' said Ravi.

example.problem: Which is bigger: 1/2 or 2/4?
example.solution: 1/2 = 2/4. They are equal; neither is bigger.

points.label: Tip
points.text: Draw or fold paper to see equivalent fractions

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount, just different names.

slides.title: Comparing Different Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi compares his chocolate bar piece (1/3) with Anaya's (1/4). 'Mine is bigger because I only divided mine into 3 pieces, but you divided yours into 4!'

points.label: Same Numerator
points.text: 1/3 > 1/4 (fewer pieces = bigger pieces)

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: 2/4 > 1/4 (more pieces taken = more chocolate)

points.label: Finding Common Denominator
points.text: Convert 1/2 and 1/3 to 3/6 and 2/6 to compare easily.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare fractions by finding common denominators or by visualizing pieces of the same whole.

slides.title: Your Fraction Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya has a ribbon 1 meter long. She cuts it into 5 equal pieces for her hair clips. Ravi asks: 'What fraction is each piece?'

points.label: Think
points.text: If 1 ribbon is cut into 5 equal pieces, each piece is __/5

slides.inSimpleWords: One ribbon, five equal pieces: each piece is 1/5.

image.alt: Your Fraction Challenge — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions in Daily Life
slides.storyContext: Anaya realized fractions are everywhere: half a glass of milk, one-third of the journey completed, two-quarter hours at school.

points.label: Milk
points.text: 1/2 cup of milk

points.label: Time
points.text: 1/3 of the day

points.label: Distance
points.text: 2/4 of the road

points.label: Recipes
points.text: 1/4 cup flour, 1/2 cup sugar

points.label: Money
points.text: 1/2 rupee, 1/4 of your pocket money

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions help us describe parts of things in real life.

image.alt: Fractions in Daily Life — Fractions

slides.title: Helping Anaya's Mother Bake
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother bakes a cake using the recipe: 1/2 cup butter, 1/4 cup milk, 3/4 cup flour. Anaya realizes measuring uses fractions constantly!

points.text: Baking requires precise fraction measurements.
Too much or too little changes the whole cake.

slides.title: Adding Simple Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi ate 1/4 of a pizza. Anaya ate 2/4 of the same pizza. Together, how much did they eat?

example.solution: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4 (add numerators, keep denominator same)

points.label: Rule
points.text: Same denominator? Add top numbers only.

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/4 plus 2/4 equals 3/4 of the pizza.

image.alt: Adding Simple Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya had 3/4 of a chocolate bar. She gave Ravi 1/4. How much does she have left? 3/4 - 1/4 = 2/4.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: Subtract numerators, keep denominator same

points.label: Check
points.text: Make sure you have enough: can't subtract 3/4 from 1/4

slides.inSimpleWords: To subtract fractions with same denominator, subtract top numbers and keep the bottom number.

slides.title: Fractions with Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Ravi ate 1/2 of a sandwich and Anaya ate 1/4 of an identical sandwich. How much did they eat together? 1/2 + 1/4 = ?

example.problem: 1/2 + 1/4 = ? (different denominators)
example.solution: Convert to same denominator: 1/2 = 2/4. Now: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4

slides.title: Proper and Improper Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya's bakery sold cakes in pieces. If someone bought 5 pieces when each whole cake had 4 pieces, that's 5/4 (more than one whole cake!).

points.label: Proper Fraction
points.text: Numerator < Denominator (less than 1 whole)

points.label: Improper Fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ Denominator (more than or equal to 1 whole)

points.label: Mixed Number
points.text: 5/4 = 1 and 1/4 (one whole plus one-quarter)

slides.inSimpleWords: 5/4 is bigger than one whole cake piece.

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Pizza Party Puzzle
slides.storyContext: They order 2 pizzas cut into 8 slices each (16 slices total). They eat 20 slices. That's 20/16 or 1 and 4/16 pizzas! They ate more than 1 whole pizza.

points.text: 20/16 is an improper fraction.
20/16 = 1 4/16 = 1 1/4 as a mixed number.

slides.title: Multiplying a Fraction by a Whole Number
slides.storyContext: Anaya has 1/4 of a chocolate bar. Ravi gives her 3 more identical bars. How much chocolate does she have now? 3 × 1/4 = 3/4.

example.problem: If Anaya has 1/4 of a bar and gets 3 more bars (4/4 each), how much does she have in total? 1/4 + 4/4 + 4/4 + 4/4 = ?
example.solution: 1/4 + 12/4 = 13/4 = 3 and 1/4 bars total

slides.title: Simplifying (Reducing) Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices: '4/8 and 1/2 are the same! We can simplify 4/8 by dividing both top and bottom by 4.'

points.label: Simplify
points.text: Divide numerator and denominator by the same number

points.label: Check
points.text: Stop when you can't divide anymore (lowest terms)

slides.inSimpleWords: Simplify a fraction by dividing top and bottom by the same number until you can't divide anymore.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Mastery
slides.storyContext: After practicing fractions everywhere they look—in recipes, ribbons, pizzas, and sandwiches—Anaya and Ravi feel confident. 'Fractions are everywhere!' says Anaya.

points.text: Fractions are essential math tools used daily.
Mastering fractions opens doors to advanced mathematics.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that fractions are parts of wholes, written with numerator and denominator, and found everywhere from cakes to ribbons to journeys.

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Number of parts we take (top)

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Total equal parts (bottom)

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Different fractions, same value

points.label: Adding
points.text: Same denominator: add numerators

points.label: Subtracting
points.text: Same denominator: subtract numerators

points.label: Simplify
points.text: Divide top and bottom by the same number

points.label: Real Life
points.text: Fractions describe portions of everything

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions name parts of a whole using two numbers.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson — Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Ravi and Anaya's Compass Adventure
hook: Two friends use a spinning compass to discover how turns create angles.

slides.title: Angles as Turns
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya explore angles by spinning, turning, and measuring all around them.

image.alt: Angles as Turns — Angles as Turns

slides.title: The Spinning Compass Game
slides.storyContext: Ravi found a toy compass on the beach. Anaya asked him to spin it slowly. 'When it completes one full turn, that's a complete angle,' she explained, pointing at how the needle went all the way around.

points.label: Complete Turn
points.text: One full spin = 360 degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: One full spin around is called 360 degrees.

slides.title: What is an Angle?
slides.storyContext: Anaya explains: 'An angle is formed when two lines meet at a point. The angle measures HOW MUCH we turn from one line to the other.'

points.label: Angle
points.text: Formed by two rays sharing an endpoint (vertex)

points.label: Vertex
points.text: The point where two rays meet

points.label: Measure
points.text: Measured in degrees (°)

points.label: Symbol
points.text: We write 45° to mean 45 degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle shows how much you turn from one direction to another.

slides.title: Ravi's Spinning Movements
slides.storyContext: Ravi stands and spins around: 'When I face north and turn to face east, I've turned 90 degrees. When I face south, I've turned 180 degrees!'

points.text: A 90-degree turn is one quarter of a full spin.
A 180-degree turn is half a full spin.

slides.title: Understanding Right Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya held the compass steady and told Ravi to spin it just one-quarter of the way. 'Stop!' she said. The needle had turned 90 degrees. 'That's a right angle,' Anaya smiled, 'like the corner of our classroom door.'

points.label: Right Angle
points.text: 90 degrees = one quarter turn

points.label: Symbol
points.text: A small square in the corner marks a right angle

points.label: Examples
points.text: Corners of books, doors, windows

points.label: Perpendicular
points.text: Two lines that form a right angle are perpendicular

slides.inSimpleWords: 90 degrees is one-quarter turn, like a door corner.

image.alt: Understanding Right Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Measuring Angles with Turns
slides.storyContext: Ravi turned the compass halfway around. Anaya counted: '180 degrees! That's a straight line, Ravi.' They realized half a turn makes a straight angle.

example.problem: If Ravi spins the compass halfway, how many degrees has he turned?
example.solution: Half a turn = 180 degrees (straight line)

points.label: Straight Angle
points.text: 180 degrees = half turn

slides.inSimpleWords: Halfway around is 180 degrees, making a straight line.

image.alt: Measuring Angles with Turns — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Acute, Right, and Obtuse Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya taught Ravi three types of angles using her arms. A small hug (arms close) = acute angle (less than 90°). Arms at a corner = right angle (90°). A big hug (arms wide) = obtuse angle (more than 90° but less than 180°).

points.label: Acute
points.text: Less than 90 degrees (small angle)

points.label: Right
points.text: Exactly 90 degrees (corner)

points.label: Obtuse
points.text: More than 90 but less than 180 degrees (wide)

points.label: Reflex
points.text: More than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: Three angle types: small, corner, or wide hug.

slides.title: Spotting Angles Everywhere at School
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya walk around their school: the corner of a book (90°), the open lid (60°), the staircase (120°), and the open window (100°).

points.text: Right angles appear in doors, corners, windows.
Acute angles appear in roof peaks and open scissors.
Obtuse angles appear in wide-open doors and fans.

slides.title: Finding Angles in Your Classroom
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya walked around their school. They found a right angle where the wall meets the floor (90°), an acute angle at the roof peak, and an obtuse angle at the open window.

example.problem: The window opens 120 degrees. Is this acute, right, or obtuse?
example.solution: 120° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it's obtuse.

points.label: Remember
points.text: 90° = right, less = acute, more = obtuse

slides.inSimpleWords: 120 degrees is wider than a corner, so it's obtuse.

image.alt: Finding Angles in Your Classroom — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool
slides.storyContext: Anaya pulled out a protractor. 'This tool measures angles!' she said. She placed it on the compass where the needle pointed and read the number: 45 degrees. Ravi marveled: 'That's exactly one-eighth of a full turn!'

points.label: Protractor
points.text: A semicircle with numbers 0-180

points.label: How to Use
points.text: Center at the angle point, align one ray at 0

points.label: Two Scales
points.text: Inner scale (0-180 left to right) and outer scale (180-0 left to right)

points.label: Read Carefully
points.text: Choose the scale that matches your angle opening

slides.inSimpleWords: A protractor measures angles using its numbered semicircle.

image.alt: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Anaya Measures Angles Precisely
slides.storyContext: Anaya uses her protractor to measure the angles of different objects: a pencil tilted at 35°, a door open at 85°, a roof peak at 60°, and a wide-open fan at 140°.

points.text: Different objects have different angle measures.
A protractor gives exact measurements.

slides.title: Estimate the Angle
slides.storyContext: Ravi opened the door slowly and asked Anaya to guess the angle without measuring. The door was open about a quarter way. 'About 90 degrees?' guessed Anaya. Ravi smiled: 'Close! It's actually 85 degrees.'

points.label: Skill
points.text: Estimating helps before you measure

slides.inSimpleWords: Try guessing angles before you measure them.

image.alt: Estimate the Angle — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Clock Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya noticed the school clock. 'The hour hand and minute hand make angles!' She calculated: at 3 o'clock, the hands make a 90-degree angle. At 6 o'clock, they make 180 degrees.

example.problem: At 3:00, what angle do the clock hands make?
example.solution: Hour hand at 3, minute hand at 12 = 90 degrees (right angle)

points.label: Clock Facts
points.text: Each hour = 30 degrees (360° ÷ 12 hours)

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make angles that change every minute.

image.alt: Clock Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Angles in Geometry Shapes
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws shapes: a square (four 90° angles), a triangle (three angles that add to 180°), and a pentagon (five angles that add to 540°).

points.label: Triangle
points.text: 3 angles that add up to 180°

points.label: Square/Rectangle
points.text: 4 angles that add up to 360° (four 90° angles)

points.label: Pentagon
points.text: 5 angles that add up to 540°

points.label: Formula
points.text: Sum of angles = (n - 2) × 180°, where n is number of sides

slides.inSimpleWords: Every shape has angles inside it, and the total depends on how many sides it has.

slides.title: Measuring Triangle Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya draws a triangle and measures its three angles: 60°, 60°, and 60°. 'They add up to 180!' she says. Then she draws another triangle with 90°, 45°, and 45°. 'This one also adds to 180!'

example.problem: A triangle has angles of 70° and 50°. What is the third angle?

slides.title: Angles in Nature and Design
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at the river flowing and Anaya at the trees. 'Branches make angles!' said Ravi. 'So do river bends,' added Anaya. They realized angles were everywhere: bird wings, roofs, ladders, and even the way people sit.

points.label: Nature
points.text: Tree branches, bird wings, petals

points.label: Design
points.text: Roofs, stairs, furniture

points.label: Body
points.text: Arms, legs, joints

points.label: Engineering
points.text: Bridges, dams, buildings use specific angles for strength

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are found in nature, buildings, and our bodies.

image.alt: Angles in Nature and Design — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Discovering Angles in Sports
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya watch a cricket match and notice: the bowler's arm angle, the batsman's swing angle, and the angle at which the ball flies through the air all matter for the sport.

points.text: Sports use angles for accuracy and power.
A good bowling angle and bat angle are crucial for scoring.

slides.title: Angles in Architecture
slides.storyContext: Anaya visits a construction site and sees: a roof peak at 60°, staircase steps at 30°, and door hinges opening at 120°. Each angle is designed for a specific purpose.

example.problem: A roof peak is 45° on one side and 45° on the other. What is the total angle of the roof peak?
example.solution: 45° + 45° = 90°, forming a right angle at the peak where both sides meet.

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Mastery
slides.storyContext: After exploring angles in clocks, shapes, nature, sports, and buildings, Ravi and Anaya have discovered that angles are everywhere and essential to understanding the world.

points.text: Angles are fundamental to geometry and real-world applications.
Measuring angles precisely is a critical skill in many fields.

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Discovery
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that angles measure turns, come in different sizes (acute, right, obtuse), and are measured in degrees using a protractor. They're everywhere!

points.label: Full Turn
points.text: 360 degrees

points.label: Half Turn
points.text: 180 degrees (straight)

points.label: Quarter Turn
points.text: 90 degrees (right angle)

points.label: Angle Types
points.text: Acute (<90°), Right (=90°), Obtuse (>90°), Reflex (>180°)

points.label: Measurement
points.text: Use a protractor to measure angles precisely

points.label: Shapes
points.text: Triangle angles add to 180°, quadrilateral angles add to 360°

points.label: All Around
points.text: Angles in nature, buildings, clocks, sports, and more

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles measure turns and are found everywhere we look.

image.alt: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Discovery — Angles as Turns

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Treasure Map Journey
hook: Two friends use distance to find a hidden treasure across their village.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Treasure Map Journey
slides.inSimpleWords: Learning to measure distance and find hidden treasures.

slides.title: The Mystery Map
slides.storyContext: Anaya's grandmother gave them an old map showing a treasure buried 'far from the village well.' But how far is 'far'? Anaya decided they needed to measure. She marked the well as the starting point and began measuring the distance using a measuring tape.

points.label: Starting Point
points.text: Well = distance zero

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance measures how far apart two places are.

image.alt: The Mystery Map — Far and Near

slides.title: What is Distance?
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked Anaya: 'Can we measure the gap between the well and that big banyan tree?' Anaya explained: 'Distance is the space between two points. It tells us how far apart things are.'

points.label: Distance
points.text: The gap between two locations

points.label: Measured
points.text: With a ruler, tape measure, or our body

points.label: Direction
points.text: Distance doesn't care if we go north, east, or sideways

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is how much space lies between two spots.

slides.title: Units of Measurement
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked: 'How do we measure distance?' Anaya showed him different tools: her handspan (short), a meter stick (1 meter), and a measuring wheel (for long distances). 'We use different units depending on what we're measuring,' she explained.

points.label: Centimeter (cm)
points.text: For small things like pencils

points.label: Meter (m)
points.text: For medium things like rooms or trees

points.label: Kilometer (km)
points.text: For long distances like between villages

slides.inSimpleWords: Use small units for near things, big units for far things.

image.alt: Units of Measurement — Far and Near

slides.title: Anaya's First Measurement
slides.storyContext: Anaya took her meter stick and walked along the path from the well toward the forest. She placed it end-to-end, counting: 'One meter, two meters, three meters...' Ravi watched and cheered each time she placed it down, marking distances on the old map with pencil dots.

points.label: Method
points.text: Repeat meter stick along a path

points.label: Count
points.text: Each placement = 1 meter

points.label: Record
points.text: Mark on map to track progress

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure by placing a stick end-to-end along the path.

slides.title: Converting Units
slides.storyContext: Anaya measured a path and found it was 500 meters long. 'That's half a kilometer!' she said happily. Ravi wrote down the conversion: 100 cm = 1 meter, and 1000 meters = 1 kilometer.

example.problem: If the path to the treasure is 2 kilometers, how many meters is that?
example.solution: 2 km × 1000 = 2000 meters

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 kilometers is 2000 meters long.

image.alt: Converting Units — Far and Near

slides.title: More Unit Conversions
slides.storyContext: Ravi practiced converting: 'If Anaya measured 3500 meters, how many kilometers and meters is that?' Anaya calculated: '3500 ÷ 1000 = 3 remainder 500, so 3 km and 500 m!' They high-fived.

example.problem: Convert 3500 meters to kilometers and meters

points.label: Shortcut
points.text: 1000 m = 1 km exactly

slides.inSimpleWords: 3500 meters equals 3 and a half kilometers.

slides.title: Measuring Real Distances
slides.storyContext: Ravi stepped out and started walking while Anaya marked points on the map. 'One step is about half a meter,' Ravi called back. By counting steps, they estimated long distances without stopping.

points.label: Body Measures
points.text: Hand span, arm length, step length

points.label: Non-standard
points.text: Useful for quick estimates

points.label: Standard Units
points.text: Meter stick gives exact measurements

slides.inSimpleWords: Our body can help estimate distances quickly.

image.alt: Measuring Real Distances — Far and Near

slides.title: Ravi's Clever Trick
slides.storyContext: 'I counted 50 of my steps to reach that tree,' said Ravi proudly. 'And each step is 0.5 meters, so the tree is 50 × 0.5 = 25 meters away!' Anaya verified with her tape measure. 'Perfect!' she exclaimed.

points.label: Estimate
points.text: Count steps and multiply by step length

points.label: Verify
points.text: Check with standard tools later

slides.inSimpleWords: Step counting helps estimate distance on the go.

slides.title: Finding the Treasure Distance
slides.storyContext: Using the map scale (1 cm on map = 10 meters real distance), Anaya measured from the well to the marked treasure spot. The map distance was 5 cm. She calculated the real distance: 5 × 10 = 50 meters.

example.problem: Map scale: 1 cm = 20 meters. Treasure is 3 cm away on map. Real distance?
example.solution: 3 cm × 20 = 60 meters (real distance)

points.label: Map Scale
points.text: Always check the scale before trusting a map

slides.inSimpleWords: Map scale helps find real distances from drawn maps.

image.alt: Finding the Treasure Distance — Far and Near

slides.title: Reading Map Scales
slides.storyContext: Anaya pointed at the map legend: 'This shows the scale. If 1 centimeter here means 10 meters in real life, then a line that looks tiny on paper could be a huge distance outside!'

points.label: Scale Bar
points.text: Shows the ratio between map and reality

points.label: Small Map
points.text: Represents large real distances

points.label: Ratio
points.text: 1:10000 means 1 cm = 10000 cm in real world

slides.inSimpleWords: Maps shrink distances into small pictures.

slides.title: Your Distance Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya asks Ravi: 'The village market is 3 kilometers away. How many steps would you need to walk there if your step is half a meter?' Ravi started counting on his fingers!
slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate how many steps for a 3 kilometer walk.

image.alt: Your Distance Challenge — Far and Near

slides.title: Comparing the Two Routes
slides.storyContext: Anaya found two possible paths to the treasure on the map. Path A looked winding (4 cm on map = 40 meters). Path B looked straighter (3 cm on map = 30 meters). 'Path B is shorter!' Ravi observed. 'Shorter routes save energy,' said Anaya wisely.

points.label: Path A
points.text: 40 meters (winding)

points.label: Path B
points.text: 30 meters (straight)

slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes the shortest distance is not the most obvious path.

slides.title: Comparing Distances
slides.storyContext: At the market, Anaya and Ravi saw signs: 'School: 2 km away' and 'River: 1500 meters away.' 'The river is nearer!' Ravi realized. '1500 meters is only 1.5 kilometers, and 1.5 < 2,' explained Anaya.

points.label: Compare
points.text: Convert to same unit before comparing

points.label: Order
points.text: Use < (less), = (equal), > (greater)

slides.inSimpleWords: First change to the same unit, then compare distances.

image.alt: Comparing Distances — Far and Near

slides.title: Ranking Three Locations
slides.storyContext: Anaya listed three distances to places in town: 'Hospital: 800 m, Library: 1.2 km, Park: 600 m.' Ravi ordered them: 'Park (600 m), Hospital (800 m), Library (1200 m) — from nearest to farthest!'

example.problem: Order these from nearest to farthest: 900 m, 1 km, 750 m

slides.inSimpleWords: Always use the same units before ordering distances.

slides.title: Perimeter: Distance Around
slides.storyContext: Anaya drew a square field on her map (each side 100 meters). Ravi asked, 'How far around the whole field?' Anaya calculated: 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 400 meters. 'That's the perimeter!' she declared.

example.problem: A rectangular garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. What's the distance around it?
example.solution: Perimeter = 2 × (8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = 26 meters

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Distance all the way around a shape

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the total distance around a shape.

image.alt: Perimeter: Distance Around — Far and Near

slides.title: Fencing the Treasure Area
slides.storyContext: When they found the treasure spot, it was a square piece of land. Ravi wanted to fence it off. 'Each side is 20 meters, so we need 20 + 20 + 20 + 20 = 80 meters of fence!' said Anaya. 'That's lots of wood!' laughed Ravi.

points.label: Total Fence
points.text: 80 meters for all four sides

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter tells us how much fence to buy.

slides.title: Distance in Time and Speed
slides.storyContext: When they finally walked to the treasure location, Ravi checked his watch: 30 minutes for 500 meters. 'We were walking at a certain speed,' Anaya said. 'Distance ÷ Time = Speed!'

points.label: Speed
points.text: How fast you move

points.label: Formula
points.text: Speed = Distance ÷ Time

points.label: Units
points.text: Meters per minute or kilometers per hour

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed tells us how far we travel in a certain time.

image.alt: Distance in Time and Speed — Far and Near

slides.title: Calculating Speed
slides.storyContext: Anaya timed Ravi running 100 meters. It took him 20 seconds. She calculated: Speed = 100 m ÷ 20 s = 5 meters per second. 'You're running fast!' she cheered.

example.problem: A car travels 120 kilometers in 2 hours. What's its speed?
example.solution: Speed = 120 km ÷ 2 hours = 60 km per hour

points.label: Formula
points.text: Speed = Distance ÷ Time

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide distance by time to find how fast something moves.

slides.title: The Treasure Hunt Race
slides.storyContext: Ravi sprinted the last 200 meters in 40 seconds. Anaya walked the same distance in 2 minutes (120 seconds). Ravi calculated: 200 ÷ 40 = 5 m/s. Anaya: 200 ÷ 120 ≈ 1.7 m/s. 'You were almost 3 times faster!' she laughed.

points.label: Sprint Speed
points.text: 5 meters per second (fast!)

points.label: Walk Speed
points.text: ~1.7 meters per second (steady)

slides.inSimpleWords: Different speeds for different activities.

slides.title: Reversing Speed to Find Distance
slides.storyContext: On the return journey, Anaya used a different formula. 'If we walk at 2 meters per second for 15 minutes, how far do we go? Distance = Speed × Time = 2 × (15 × 60 seconds) = 2 × 900 = 1800 meters!'

points.label: Formula
points.text: Distance = Speed × Time

points.label: Rearranged
points.text: If Speed = Distance ÷ Time, then Distance = Speed × Time

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply speed by time to get distance traveled.

slides.title: Finding Distance from Speed
slides.storyContext: A cyclist rides at 15 km per hour for 3 hours. Ravi calculated: Distance = 15 × 3 = 45 kilometers. 'That's how far the cyclist travels!' said Anaya.

example.problem: A train travels at 80 km/h for 5 hours. How far does it go?
example.solution: Distance = 80 × 5 = 400 kilometers

points.label: Remember
points.text: Faster speed × longer time = greater distance

slides.inSimpleWords: 80 km per hour for 5 hours = 400 km total.

slides.title: Speed and Distance Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya asks: 'If a bus travels 120 kilometers in 4 hours, what's its speed? And if it keeps going at that speed for 6 hours, how far will it travel?'

points.label: Think
points.text: Speed = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 km/h; Distance = 30 × 6 = 180 km

slides.inSimpleWords: Use both formulas: find speed first, then new distance.

slides.title: Real-World Distances and Scales
slides.storyContext: Back at home, Anaya created a scale model. 'If our village is 10 km across, and my model is 1 meter across, then 1 meter on my model = 10 km in real life!' She shrunk huge distances into a tiny, hold-able model.

points.label: Scale Model
points.text: Miniature version using proportions

points.label: Real Distance
points.text: Much larger than the model

points.label: Ratio
points.text: Model scale maintains true proportions

slides.inSimpleWords: Scale models show real-world sizes in tiny form.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Treasure Discovery
slides.storyContext: They found the treasure and realized distance shapes our world: maps, journeys, measurements, and speeds all depend on understanding far and near.

points.label: Units
points.text: cm, m, km for different distances

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Distance around a shape

points.label: Speed
points.text: Distance ÷ Time; Distance = Speed × Time

points.label: Maps & Models
points.text: Scales shrink real distances into readable sizes

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is how far apart things are and how we measure.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Treasure Discovery — Far and Near

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Dairy Adventure
hook: Two friends help a farmer divide milk and count costs at a dairy farm.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Dairy Adventure
slides.inSimpleWords: Learning to divide, multiply, and solve farm problems.

slides.title: Welcome to the Dairy Farm
slides.storyContext: Anaya's uncle owns a dairy farm with 24 cows. He asked the children to help organize the milk bottles into crates. Anaya asked: 'How many bottles fit in each crate if we want them divided equally?'

points.label: Problem
points.text: 24 bottles ÷ 6 crates = ? bottles per crate

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing things equally helps us share fairly.

image.alt: Welcome to the Dairy Farm — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Division: Sharing Equally
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya packed bottles into 6 crates: 4 in the first, 4 in the second, 4 in the third... 'Each crate has 4 bottles! That's fair,' Anaya realized. '24 ÷ 6 = 4,' she wrote.

points.label: Division Symbol
points.text: ÷ means 'divided by' or 'shared into'

points.label: Dividend
points.text: The number being divided (24)

points.label: Divisor
points.text: Number of groups (6)

points.label: Quotient
points.text: Answer to the division (4)

slides.inSimpleWords: Division splits things fairly into equal groups.

image.alt: Division: Sharing Equally — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Dividing the Bottles
slides.storyContext: Anaya methodically placed bottles into the crates, one by one. 'One... four bottles in crate A. One... four bottles in crate B.' Ravi counted: '6 groups of 4 = 24 bottles total. Perfect division, no leftover!'

points.label: Equal Groups
points.text: Each crate gets the same amount

points.label: No Remainder
points.text: 24 ÷ 6 divides evenly

slides.inSimpleWords: Division means fair sharing with no leftovers.

slides.title: Division with Remainders
slides.storyContext: The next day, 28 liters of milk arrived, and Anaya wanted to fill bottles that hold 5 liters each. 'How many full bottles, and any milk left over?' asked Ravi. They calculated: 28 ÷ 5 = 5 full bottles with 3 liters remaining.

example.problem: Divide 28 liters into 5-liter bottles. How many full bottles and remainder?
example.solution: 28 ÷ 5 = 5 remainder 3 (5 full bottles, 3 liters left)

points.label: Remainder
points.text: The amount left after equal division

slides.inSimpleWords: 28 ÷ 5 makes 5 full bottles with 3 liters extra.

image.alt: Division with Remainders — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: More Division with Remainders
slides.storyContext: Ravi tried another problem: '35 cookies to share among 8 friends. How many per friend and how many left?' Anaya calculated: 35 ÷ 8 = 4 remainder 3. 'Each friend gets 4 cookies, and 3 are left for the cat!' she joked.

example.problem: 35 ÷ 8 = ? remainder ?
example.solution: 35 ÷ 8 = 4 remainder 3 (because 8 × 4 = 32, and 35 - 32 = 3)

points.label: Check
points.text: Divisor × Quotient + Remainder = Dividend

slides.inSimpleWords: Remainders show what doesn't divide evenly.

slides.title: Multiplication and Division: Opposites
slides.storyContext: Anaya showed Ravi a clever trick. 'If 6 crates × 4 bottles = 24 bottles, then 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Multiplication and division undo each other!' She wrote: 6 × 4 = 24 AND 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

points.label: Inverse Operation
points.text: Multiplication ↔ Division

points.label: Check Division
points.text: Multiply quotient by divisor to verify

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply to combine groups; divide to separate groups.

image.alt: Multiplication and Division: Opposites — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Using Multiplication to Check Division
slides.storyContext: Anaya claimed: '30 bottles ÷ 5 crates = 6 bottles per crate.' Ravi verified: 'Let me check: 5 crates × 6 bottles = 30 bottles. Correct!' He nodded approvingly.

points.label: Verification
points.text: Multiply to confirm division answer

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply to check if a division answer is correct.

slides.title: Calculating Costs at the Dairy
slides.storyContext: Each bottle of milk costs 30 rupees. The farm sold 15 bottles. Ravi calculated: 15 × 30 = 450 rupees. But when a customer returned 5 bottles for a refund, Anaya divided: 450 ÷ 3 = 150 rupees (5 × 30).

example.problem: If milk is 30 rupees per bottle, how much for 8 bottles?
example.solution: 8 × 30 = 240 rupees

points.label: Repeated Addition
points.text: Multiplication is quicker than adding many times

slides.inSimpleWords: 8 bottles at 30 rupees each costs 240 rupees.

image.alt: Calculating Costs at the Dairy — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Bulk Purchase Problem
slides.storyContext: A restaurant orders 12 crates of milk, and each crate costs 500 rupees. Ravi multiplied: 12 × 500 = 6000 rupees. 'That's a big order!' he whistled.

example.problem: 12 crates at 500 rupees each = ? total

points.label: Bulk Purchase
points.text: More items = higher total cost

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply quantity by price per unit to find total cost.

slides.title: Your Farm Math Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya's uncle has 72 square meters of pasture land. He wants to divide it equally among his 8 cows for grazing. How much space does each cow get? (Hint: Use division!)

points.label: Think
points.text: 72 ÷ 8 = ? square meters per cow

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide 72 by 8 to find space for each cow.

image.alt: Your Farm Math Challenge — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Grouping and Counting in Rows and Columns
slides.storyContext: Anaya arranged milk bottles on a shelf in 3 rows and 4 columns. 'That's 3 × 4 = 12 bottles total,' she said. Ravi rearranged them into 2 rows and 6 columns. 'Still 2 × 6 = 12 bottles, same amount, different shape!'

points.label: Array
points.text: Bottles arranged in rows and columns

points.label: Commutative
points.text: 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 (order doesn't change product)

slides.inSimpleWords: Rows times columns give the total, even if arranged differently.

image.alt: Grouping and Counting in Rows and Columns — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Rearranging the Bottles
slides.storyContext: Anaya showed Ravi something cool: 'Look, 5 rows of 3 bottles is 15. But if I flip it, 3 rows of 5 bottles is also 15! Multiplication doesn't care about order!' Ravi's eyes lit up.

points.label: Property
points.text: Commutative property of multiplication

slides.inSimpleWords: You can multiply in any order and get the same answer.

slides.title: Word Problems from the Farm
slides.storyContext: The dairy worker has 36 bottle crates. He packs them into boxes that hold 9 crates each. Ravi questions: 'How many boxes does he need?' Anaya responds: '36 ÷ 9 = 4 boxes.'

example.problem: 36 crates ÷ 9 crates per box = ? boxes
example.solution: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 boxes needed

points.label: Verify
points.text: Check: 4 × 9 = 36 (correct!)

slides.inSimpleWords: 36 crates divide evenly into 4 boxes of 9 each.

image.alt: Word Problems from the Farm — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Two-Step Farm Problem
slides.storyContext: Anaya's uncle sells milk to 3 stores. Each store gets 24 bottles. How many bottles total? Anaya: 3 × 24 = 72 bottles. Then Ravi asks: 'If he has 120 bottles total, how many left after the delivery?' Anaya: 120 - 72 = 48 bottles.

example.problem: Multiply: 3 stores × 24 bottles each. Then subtract from 120 total.
example.solution: 3 × 24 = 72 sold; 120 - 72 = 48 remaining

points.label: Multiple Steps
points.text: Do multiplication first, then subtraction

slides.inSimpleWords: Break big problems into smaller steps.

slides.title: Division Patterns and Times Tables
slides.storyContext: Anaya noticed patterns in the dairy: '6 × 5 = 30, so 30 ÷ 5 = 6. When we know times tables, division is easy!' They practiced: 7 × 8 = 56, so 56 ÷ 8 = 7.

points.label: Times Tables
points.text: Help us divide quickly

points.label: Pattern
points.text: If a × b = c, then c ÷ b = a

slides.inSimpleWords: Knowing multiplication helps us divide faster.

image.alt: Division Patterns and Times Tables — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: The Times Table Trick
slides.storyContext: Ravi recited: '3 × 7 = 21, so 21 ÷ 7 = 3. And 4 × 9 = 36, so 36 ÷ 4 = 9!' Anaya was impressed. 'You're using times tables backwards!' she laughed.

points.label: Forward
points.text: Multiplication: a × b = c

points.label: Backward
points.text: Division: c ÷ b = a

slides.inSimpleWords: Every multiplication fact gives you two division facts.

slides.title: Dividing Groups into Smaller Groups
slides.storyContext: The farm has 48 bottles. Anaya wanted to pack them into 6 boxes equally. '48 ÷ 6 = 8 bottles per box.' Then Ravi asked: 'What if we divide those 8 bottles further into 2-bottle packs?' So: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 packs per box. Total: 6 × 4 = 24 packs!

points.label: First Division
points.text: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 bottles per box

points.label: Second Division
points.text: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 smaller packs

slides.inSimpleWords: You can divide groups, then divide again.

slides.title: Organizing the Shipment
slides.storyContext: The farm ships milk to the city weekly. Anaya's uncle had 144 bottles to package. 'We need 12 boxes. Each box gets 144 ÷ 12 = 12 bottles. Each bottle costs 25 rupees, so total value = 144 × 25 = 3600 rupees!' calculated Ravi excitedly.

points.label: Divide for Groups
points.text: 144 ÷ 12 = 12 bottles per box

points.label: Multiply for Total
points.text: 144 × 25 = 3600 rupees total value

slides.inSimpleWords: Organize shipments with division and multiplication.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Dairy Farm Lessons
slides.storyContext: The children learned that division shares things fairly, multiplication and division are opposites, and both help us solve real problems on the farm.

points.label: Division
points.text: Splits into equal groups (÷)

points.label: Remainder
points.text: What's left after dividing equally

points.label: Inverse
points.text: Multiplication ↔ Division

points.label: Arrays
points.text: Rows × Columns = Total (any order works)

points.label: Real Use
points.text: Farm costs, bottles, groups, and sharing

slides.inSimpleWords: Division and multiplication solve real farm problems.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Dairy Farm Lessons — The Dairy Farm

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Pattern Discovery
hook: Two friends find shapes and patterns everywhere in their town.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Pattern Discovery
slides.inSimpleWords: Exploring shapes, patterns, and symmetry all around us.

slides.title: Shapes in the Market
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi visited the village market. Anaya pointed: 'Look at all the shapes! Round tomatoes, square baskets, rectangular boxes!' Ravi replied, 'I see patterns too — the baskets are stacked in rows and columns.'

points.label: Observation
points.text: Shapes and patterns surround us daily

slides.inSimpleWords: Our world is full of shapes arranged in patterns.

image.alt: Shapes in the Market — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: The Hunt Begins
slides.storyContext: Ravi brought a notebook to sketch shapes. 'Look, Anaya! The baker's bread is round. That window is square. The temple roof is triangular!' Anaya smiled: 'Let's explore the whole town and catalog every shape we find.'

points.label: Round
points.text: Bread, plates, clocks

points.label: Square/Rectangular
points.text: Windows, doors, books

points.label: Triangular
points.text: Roofs, flags, trees

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes appear everywhere in our homes and towns.

slides.title: 2D Shapes: Flat and Drawn
slides.storyContext: Anaya drew shapes on the ground with a stick. 'Triangle has 3 sides, square has 4 equal sides, circle has no corners, and rectangle has 4 sides but not all equal,' she explained, drawing each one.

points.label: Triangle
points.text: 3 sides, 3 corners (vertices)

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: 4 sides, opposite sides equal, 4 right angles

points.label: Circle
points.text: No sides, no corners, perfectly round

slides.inSimpleWords: 2D shapes are flat with sides and corners.

image.alt: 2D Shapes: Flat and Drawn — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Naming More 2D Shapes
slides.storyContext: Anaya discovered more shapes: a pentagon (5 sides, like a house outline), a hexagon (6 sides, like a honeycomb cell), and an octagon (8 sides, like a stop sign). 'Each shape is named by its number of sides!' she exclaimed.

example.problem: What do we call a shape with 6 sides?
example.solution: Hexagon (hex = 6)

points.label: Pentagon
points.text: 5 sides

points.label: Hexagon
points.text: 6 sides

points.label: Octagon
points.text: 8 sides

slides.inSimpleWords: The number of sides tells you the shape's name.

slides.title: Finding Perimeter of Shapes
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked Anaya to find the distance around a triangular vegetable patch. One side was 5 meters, the second was 4 meters, and the third was 6 meters. Anaya added: 5 + 4 + 6 = 15 meters (perimeter).

example.problem: Triangle sides: 5 m, 4 m, 6 m. What's the perimeter?
example.solution: 5 + 4 + 6 = 15 meters

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Add all sides to get the distance around

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the total distance around any shape.

image.alt: Finding Perimeter of Shapes — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Measuring Around Shapes
slides.storyContext: Anaya measured around a square market stall: each side was 2 meters. 'The perimeter is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 meters.' Ravi noted: 'That's also 4 × 2 = 8!' They discovered a shortcut for squares.

points.label: Square Perimeter
points.text: Side length × 4

slides.inSimpleWords: For a square, multiply one side by 4.

slides.title: 3D Shapes: Solid and Real
slides.storyContext: Ravi picked up an apple (sphere), a gift box (cube), and a carrot (cone). 'These are 3D shapes! They have length, width, and height. We can hold them!' Anaya listed more: cylinder (water pipe), pyramid (temple roof), and cuboid (brick).

points.label: Cube
points.text: 6 square faces, like a die

points.label: Sphere
points.text: Perfectly round, like a ball

points.label: Cylinder
points.text: Tube shape, circular tops and bottom

points.label: Pyramid
points.text: Pointed, triangular faces meeting at apex

points.label: Cuboid
points.text: Like a cube but rectangular

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D shapes are solid and take up real space.

image.alt: 3D Shapes: Solid and Real — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Finding 3D Shapes at Home
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi explored their homes. 'The sugar box is a cube! The glass is a cylinder! The pencil is like a... cuboid!' Ravi laughed. 'Even ice cream cones are cones!' They realized 3D shapes were everywhere.

points.label: Cube
points.text: Boxes, dice, sugar containers

points.label: Cylinder
points.text: Glasses, cans, pillars

points.label: Sphere
points.text: Balls, oranges, planets

slides.inSimpleWords: Every object around us is a 3D shape.

slides.title: Nets: Unfolding 3D Shapes
slides.storyContext: Anaya unfolded a cardboard box to show Ravi the net. 'If we unfold this cube, we get 6 squares! Folding them back makes the box again,' she demonstrated carefully.

example.problem: A cube's net shows 6 square faces. When folded, what shape forms?
example.solution: A cube (all 6 faces form a closed 3D shape)

points.label: Net
points.text: Flat unfolded version of a 3D shape

slides.inSimpleWords: Nets are flat patterns that fold into solid shapes.

image.alt: Nets: Unfolding 3D Shapes — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Nets of Other 3D Shapes
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked: 'What's the net of a cylinder?' Anaya drew it: 'Two circles (top and bottom) and a rectangle (the curved side, flattened).' For a pyramid: 'One square base and 4 triangles.'

example.problem: How many faces does a pyramid net have?
example.solution: 5 faces (1 square base + 4 triangular sides)

points.label: Cylinder Net
points.text: 2 circles + 1 rectangle

points.label: Pyramid Net
points.text: 1 square + 4 triangles

slides.inSimpleWords: Different 3D shapes unfold into different net patterns.

slides.title: Patterns and Sequences
slides.storyContext: On the temple wall, Anaya found a repeating pattern: square, circle, triangle, square, circle, triangle... 'It repeats every 3 shapes!' said Ravi. They also noticed number patterns: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (adding 2 each time).

points.label: Repeating Pattern
points.text: Core unit repeats (shape, color, or number)

points.label: Growing Pattern
points.text: Each element increases by a fixed amount

points.label: Rule
points.text: The pattern follows a clear rule

slides.inSimpleWords: Patterns repeat or grow following a rule.

image.alt: Patterns and Sequences — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Creating a Pattern
slides.storyContext: Anaya arranged beads on a string: red, red, blue, red, red, blue... 'Every third bead is blue!' she noticed. Ravi tried: green, green, green, yellow, green, green, green, yellow... 'Every 4th bead is yellow!'

points.label: Repeating Unit
points.text: The core that repeats over and over

slides.inSimpleWords: Find the unit that repeats in a pattern.

slides.title: Identifying Pattern Rules
slides.storyContext: Anaya wrote: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. 'The pattern adds 3 each time,' said Ravi. 'Or multiplies by 3 from the position! First: 1×3, Second: 2×3, Third: 3×3,' said Anaya.

example.problem: Pattern: 3, 6, 9, 12, ?, ?. What are the next two numbers?
example.solution: 15, 18 (add 3 to each number)

points.label: Rule
points.text: Each term = 3 × position number

slides.inSimpleWords: Pattern: 3, 6, 9... continues by adding 3 each time.

image.alt: Identifying Pattern Rules — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Finding Missing Numbers in Patterns
slides.storyContext: Ravi gave Anaya a puzzle: 2, 4, 6, ?, 10. 'That's easy!' Anaya said. 'It's adding 2 each time, so the missing number is 8.' Ravi smiled: '5, 10, 15, 20, ?, 30. What's missing?' Anaya: '25! Add 5 each time.'

example.problem: 5, 10, 15, 20, ?, 30 — find the missing number
example.solution: 25 (each number adds 5 more)

points.label: Identify Rule
points.text: Find what adds (or multiplies) each time

points.label: Apply Rule
points.text: Use it to find missing numbers

slides.inSimpleWords: Understand the rule to find missing numbers.

slides.title: Your Pattern Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws a pattern on the ground: red circle, blue square, red circle, blue square... What comes next? And if the pattern starts again, how many shapes until we see two red circles in a row?

points.label: Think
points.text: Identify the rule, predict the next shape, count carefully

slides.inSimpleWords: Figure out pattern rules and predict what comes next.

image.alt: Your Pattern Challenge — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Symmetry and Reflection
slides.storyContext: Anaya folded a sheet of paper and drew a butterfly outline. When she unfolded it, a perfect butterfly appeared. 'It's symmetrical! Both sides are identical mirror images,' she exclaimed. Ravi found symmetry in a folded square and a circle.

points.label: Line of Symmetry
points.text: An imaginary line where we fold for two equal halves

points.label: Symmetrical
points.text: Both sides are identical mirror images

points.label: Examples
points.text: Butterfly wings, temple doors, flower petals

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetrical shapes have two identical mirrored halves.

image.alt: Symmetry and Reflection — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Finding Symmetry Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi looked for symmetrical shapes in town. 'The temple has a vertical line of symmetry down the middle!' said Ravi. Anaya found: 'Human faces are symmetrical, flowers often are, and many letters too!' They drew lines of symmetry on each.

points.label: Vertical
points.text: Up-down symmetry

points.label: Horizontal
points.text: Left-right symmetry

points.label: Both
points.text: Some shapes have multiple lines of symmetry

slides.inSimpleWords: Many things in nature are perfectly symmetrical.

slides.title: Counting Lines of Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Anaya drew shapes and counted symmetry lines: 'A square has 4 lines (vertical, horizontal, and 2 diagonals). A rectangle has 2 (vertical and horizontal). A circle has infinite lines — any line through the center works!' Ravi was amazed.

example.problem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
example.solution: 4 lines (2 through opposite corners, 2 through opposite sides)

points.label: Triangle
points.text: Equilateral has 3 lines; isosceles has 1

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 lines of symmetry

points.label: Circle
points.text: Infinite lines of symmetry

slides.inSimpleWords: Some shapes have many lines of symmetry.

slides.title: Rotation and Pattern Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Ravi drew a pattern with flowers: one flower pointing up. He rotated it 90°, then 180°, then 270° around a center point. 'Look, the pattern repeats after every rotation!' Anaya realized: 'This is rotational symmetry!'

points.label: Rotational Symmetry
points.text: Shape looks the same when rotated

points.label: Center Point
points.text: The point around which we rotate

points.label: Angle
points.text: 90°, 180°, 270° rotations

slides.inSimpleWords: Some shapes look the same when spun around.

slides.title: Designing with Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Anaya created a mandala (circular design) with perfect rotational symmetry. 'If I rotate this 45 degrees, it looks the same! And again at 90 degrees!' Ravi helped color sections, confident they'd repeat perfectly.

points.label: Design Principle
points.text: Symmetry creates beauty and balance

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry is used to create beautiful designs.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Shape and Pattern Journey
slides.storyContext: They learned that shapes (2D and 3D) are everywhere, patterns repeat or grow by rules, and symmetry creates beauty in nature and design.

points.label: 2D Shapes
points.text: Triangle, square, rectangle, circle, pentagon, hexagon (flat)

points.label: 3D Shapes
points.text: Cube, sphere, cylinder, pyramid, cuboid (solid)

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Distance around a shape (add all sides)

points.label: Patterns
points.text: Repeat, grow, or follow a rule

points.label: Symmetry
points.text: Reflect perfectly or rotate symmetrically

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes, patterns, and symmetry shape our beautiful world.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Shape and Pattern Journey — Shapes and Patterns

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Kitchen Experiment
hook: Two friends discover how to measure weight and capacity at home.

characters.name: Anaya
characters.role: chef in training who measures ingredients

slides.title: Baking a Cake with Math
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother was baking a cake and asked the children to weigh flour and measure milk. Anaya found the kitchen scale and milk measuring cup. 'So weight measures how heavy, and capacity measures how much liquid fits!' she realized.

points.label: Weight
points.text: How heavy something is

points.label: Capacity
points.text: How much a container can hold

slides.inSimpleWords: Weight and capacity help us cook recipes correctly.

image.alt: Baking a Cake with Math — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Units of Weight
slides.storyContext: Ravi placed flour on the scale. 'It says 250 grams,' he read aloud. Anaya pointed to a bag of rice: '2 kilograms. That's much heavier!' She explained: 1000 grams = 1 kilogram.

points.label: Gram (g)
points.text: Small unit for light things (pencil, coins)

points.label: Kilogram (kg)
points.text: Larger unit for heavier things (people, bags)

slides.inSimpleWords: Grams for light things, kilograms for heavy things.

image.alt: Units of Weight — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Comparing Weights in the Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi started weighing everything. A pencil: 5 grams. A banana: 120 grams. A full water bottle: 1 kilogram. 'Look how different weights can be!' said Ravi. Anaya nodded: 'That's why we need both grams for tiny things and kilograms for big things.'

points.label: Small Objects
points.text: Measured in grams (light items)

points.label: Large Objects
points.text: Measured in kilograms (heavy items)

slides.inSimpleWords: Different items weigh very different amounts.

slides.title: Weighing Recipe Ingredients
slides.storyContext: The cake recipe needed: 200g flour, 100g sugar, 50g butter, and 200ml milk. Ravi weighed each. 'Total weight of dry ingredients: 200 + 100 + 50 = 350 grams!' he calculated.

example.problem: Recipe needs 200g flour + 100g sugar + 50g butter. Total dry weight?

points.label: Remember
points.text: Add weights carefully using the same unit

slides.inSimpleWords: Total ingredients: 200 + 100 + 50 = 350 grams.

image.alt: Weighing Recipe Ingredients — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Practical Weight Ranges
slides.storyContext: Anaya made a reference list: A sheet of paper weighs 5g. A banana weighs 100-150g. A kilogram is like 10 bananas together. This helped them estimate weights without always using the scale.

points.label: Light Items
points.text: 1-100g (coins, pencils, apples)

points.label: Medium Items
points.text: 100g-1kg (bananas, vegetables, water bottles)

points.label: Heavy Items
points.text: Above 1kg (bags of rice, people, furniture)

slides.inSimpleWords: Learn common weights to estimate quickly.

slides.title: Units of Capacity (Volume)
slides.storyContext: Anaya poured milk into a measuring cup marked with milliliters (ml). 'This measures how much liquid,' she said. She filled it to 250ml. Ravi asked about liters. 'One liter bottle holds 1000 milliliters!'

points.label: Milliliter (ml)
points.text: Small unit for small amounts of liquid

points.label: Liter (L)
points.text: Larger unit for bigger amounts

slides.inSimpleWords: Milliliters measure small amounts, liters measure big amounts.

image.alt: Units of Capacity (Volume) — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Measuring Liquids at Home
slides.storyContext: Ravi filled different containers: a teaspoon was 5ml, a cup was 250ml, a water bottle was 1 liter. 'Everything holds a different amount!' he said. Anaya added: 'But we can always compare them using the same units.'

points.label: Teaspoon
points.text: About 5 ml

points.label: Cup
points.text: About 250 ml

points.label: Bottle
points.text: About 1 liter

slides.inSimpleWords: Kitchen containers hold different amounts of liquid.

slides.title: Converting and Comparing Capacities
slides.storyContext: Anaya had a 2-liter bottle of juice and a 500ml measuring cup. 'How many times can I fill the cup from the bottle?' Ravi calculated: 2 L = 2000 ml, so 2000 ÷ 500 = 4 times!

example.problem: How many 250ml glasses fit in a 2L milk bottle?
example.solution: 2000 ml ÷ 250 ml = 8 glasses

points.label: Tip
points.text: Convert to the same unit before dividing

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 liters fills eight 250ml glasses.

image.alt: Converting and Comparing Capacities — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Weighing Different Objects
slides.storyContext: In the kitchen, Anaya and Ravi weighed various items. A lemon: 50g. An apple: 150g. A watermelon: 3 kg. A handful of lentils: 25g. They realized weights vary greatly depending on the item.

points.label: Light Objects
points.text: Use grams (pencil, coin, spoon)

points.label: Heavy Objects
points.text: Use kilograms (person, bag of rice)

points.label: Estimation
points.text: Practice guessing weights before weighing

slides.inSimpleWords: Different objects have very different weights.

image.alt: Weighing Different Objects — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Weight Problems in Daily Life
slides.storyContext: Ravi's dad was packing groceries. He carried 2kg rice, 1kg lentils, and a light bag of salt. 'This is getting heavy!' he said. Anaya helped: 'We're carrying 3 kilograms together. That's like 30 bananas!'

points.label: Adding Weights
points.text: 2kg + 1kg = 3kg

points.label: Weight Comparison
points.text: Estimate using familiar objects

slides.inSimpleWords: We add and compare weights in everyday tasks.

slides.title: Capacity Problem-Solving
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother asked: 'I need 500ml milk for tea and 250ml for smoothie. Do I have enough from a 1-liter carton?' Anaya calculated: 500 + 250 = 750ml. 'Yes! And 250ml is left over,' she said proudly.

points.label: Finding Total
points.text: Add capacities using same unit

points.label: Leftover
points.text: Subtract used from total

slides.inSimpleWords: We solve liquid measurement problems step by step.

slides.title: Your Kitchen Math Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother has a 5-kilogram bag of sugar. She uses 250 grams for one cake. How many cakes can she make? (Hint: Convert to the same unit first!)
slides.inSimpleWords: How many 250g cakes fit in 5 kilograms?

image.alt: Your Kitchen Math Challenge — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Weight and Capacity in Daily Life
slides.storyContext: Ravi noted what they used weight and capacity for: measuring milk for tea (capacity), weighing rice for lunch (weight), checking if the baby gained weight (weight), and filling a water bottle for school (capacity).

example.problem: Mom needs 500g flour and 250ml milk for a recipe. Has she enough from 1kg flour and 1L milk?

points.label: Real Use
points.text: Cooking, shopping, health, and storage

slides.inSimpleWords: Weight and capacity help in cooking and shopping.

image.alt: Weight and Capacity in Daily Life — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Baking the Perfect Cake
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi finally had their turn to bake. 'Remember: 200g flour, 100g sugar, 100g butter, 200ml milk, and 2 eggs!' Ravi carefully measured each ingredient. The cake turned out perfect because they used the exact amounts.

points.label: Precision
points.text: Exact measurements make recipes work

points.label: Practice
points.text: Get faster and better with each try

slides.inSimpleWords: Correct measurements make great cakes every time.

slides.title: Relationship Between Weight and Capacity
slides.storyContext: Anaya discovered something interesting: 1 liter of water weighs 1 kilogram! 'So 500ml of water weighs 500 grams!' she exclaimed. This only works for water; oil and honey weigh differently.

points.label: Water
points.text: 1L water = 1 kg (or 1000 ml = 1000 g)

points.label: Other Liquids
points.text: May have different weights per volume

points.label: Density
points.text: Different liquids have different densities

slides.inSimpleWords: One liter of water weighs one kilogram.

image.alt: Relationship Between Weight and Capacity — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Exploring Density with Ravi
slides.storyContext: Ravi filled one bottle with water and another with oil, same size. 'The water is heavier!' he said. Anaya nodded: 'Water is denser than oil. Oil actually floats on water because it's lighter for the same volume.'

points.label: Density
points.text: How heavy something is for its size

points.label: Water
points.text: Denser than oil

slides.inSimpleWords: Some liquids are heavier than others in the same container.

slides.title: Real-World Weight and Capacity
slides.storyContext: At the grocery store: Rice (by weight in kg), Milk (by volume in liters), Butter (by weight in grams). 'Everything is labeled by weight or capacity!' Ravi pointed out. 'That's how stores tell us how much we're getting.'

example.problem: A 2kg bag of rice costs Rs 150. A 1kg bag costs Rs 80. Which is better value?
example.solution: 2kg for Rs 150 = Rs 75 per kg. 1kg for Rs 80 = Rs 80 per kg. The 2kg bag is cheaper per kilogram.

points.label: Comparison
points.text: Weight helps compare value for money

slides.inSimpleWords: Weight and capacity labels help us shop smart.

slides.title: Common Conversions to Remember
slides.storyContext: Anaya made a quick-reference card: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 L = 1000 ml, 1 teaspoon ≈ 5 ml, 1 cup ≈ 250 ml. 'These help when I don't have exact measuring tools!' she said.

points.label: Kitchen Measures
points.text: 1 teaspoon ≈ 5 ml, 1 cup ≈ 250 ml

slides.inSimpleWords: Learn these conversions for quick problem-solving.

slides.title: Measurement Challenge: Mixing Recipes
slides.storyContext: Ravi wants to double a recipe. Original: 150g flour, 100g sugar, 250ml milk. What are the new measurements? (Double each one!)
slides.inSimpleWords: Double a recipe by doubling each ingredient.

slides.title: Teaching Their Friends
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi showed their friends how to measure. 'Weight tells us how heavy, capacity tells us how full!' they explained. Soon everyone could measure ingredients correctly.

points.label: Teaching
points.text: Sharing knowledge helps others learn

slides.inSimpleWords: Teach others what you've learned about measurement.

slides.title: Filling and Weighing a Container
